questionStem: A 19-year-old woman comes for a routine follow-up examination for acne vulgaris. She is sexually active and does not use contraception. She has had chronic migraines over the past 3 years. She has a history of early signs of cataracts. There is a family history of hypercholesterolemia and inflammatory bowel disease. Examination shows active acne vulgaris on her face. She says that the various treatments she has received have failed to adequately control her acne, and she asks for a prescription for isotretinoin, a medication that has worked well for many of her friends. Isotretinoin therapy is contraindicated in this patient because of which of the following historic findings?

choices.D: Family history of inflammatory bowel disease

correctExplanation: Isotretinoin (retinoic acid), a derivative of vitamin A, is teratogenic to the fetus and causes multiple malformations often involving the central nervous and musculoskeletal systems. Patients taking isotretinoin for acne vulgaris should be instructed to use at least one form, ideally two forms, of contraception to prevent pregnancy and resulting teratogenic consequences for the fetus. Generally, barrier methods are considered inadequate given higher failure rates; intrauterine devices and oral contraceptive pills are preferred. The patient is sexually active without the current use of contraception, which is a contraindication to using isotretinoin.
incorrectExplanation: Chronic migraines, early cataracts, hypercholesterolemia, and inflammatory bowel disease (Choices A, B, C, and D) are not characteristically exacerbated by the use of vitamin A derivatives and would not contraindicate the use of isotretinoin therapy in this patient.

questionStem: A 73-year-old man with hypertension is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 1 hour after the onset of moderate chest pain and difficulty breathing. Aspirin was administered en route to the hospital. He takes no other medications. On arrival, he is diaphoretic. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 185/min and thready, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 85/45 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygen by face mask shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Breath sounds are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm. A rhythm strip shows a wide complex tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.B: Administration of nitroglycerin by intravenous drip

correctExplanation: Patients with wide-complex (QRS greater than 120 msec) tachycardia require emergent medical attention and intervention. Rapid electrical depolarization of the heart and resultant increased heart rate impairs diastolic filling time resulting in low cardiac output leading to hypotension. Such a condition is accompanied by the high likelihood of degeneration to ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. Any patient with an unstable, wide-complex tachycardia requires immediate synchronized cardioversion to abort the rhythm and permit improved cardiac output. Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) protocols are well-established for such cases; unstable patients (hypotensive, diaphoretic, tachypneic, with altered mental status) should be immediately cardioverted. Stable, perfusing wide-complex arrhythmias (normotensive, minimally symptomatic, with easily palpable pulses) can be treated with antiarrhythmic medication. As well, any patient with pulseless wide-complex tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation should receive cardiopulmonary resuscitation and be defibrillated.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Administration of esmolol (Choice A) may be appropriate for refractory ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation but would only be used following failure of conventional ACLS protocols. Classically, it is used to rapidly lower blood pressure and heart rate in aortic dissection.

Administration of nitroglycerin by intravenous drip (Choice B) would be an appropriate choice for hypertensive emergency, refractory anginal chest pain, or as adjunct usage with a beta blocker to lower blood pressure in settings of aortic dissection.

Intravenous administration of morphine (Choice C) is appropriate for treating acute pain; however, it may worsen hemodynamics in an unstable patient.

Endotracheal intubation (Choice D) may be necessary for airway protection in a patient with depressed mental status, but this patient is showing no immediate signs of airway compromise; his respiratory symptoms are more likely explained by hypoperfusion which should be addressed immediately.

questionStem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of ripping substernal chest pain. She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. Her blood pressure is 220/128 mm Hg in both arms. Carotid, radial, femoral, and pedal pulses are within normal limits. An x-ray of the chest shows a widened aortic root and dilated ascending aorta. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.A: Aortic dissection due to Takayasu arteritis
choices.B: Degeneration of the aortic wall from Marfan syndrome
choices.D: Rupture of a sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
choices.E: Traumatic disruption of the aorta from a fall

correctExplanation: A history of chronic hypertension, especially if poorly controlled, along with acute, tearing, substernal chest pain is suggestive of aortic dissection. The tearing of the tunica intima and media in dissection allows for the creation of a false lumen in which blood can accumulate. Further, branch vessels can become occluded by the false lumen leading to end-organ ischemia. In older patients with a history of hypertension, atherosclerotic disease of the vasa vasorum plus breakdown of normal mural collagen and elastin results in accumulation of basophilic ground substance in place of normal tissue architecture. This process is known as cystic medial necrosis of the aorta. This process occurs predominantly in the tunica media – the smooth muscle layer of the arterial wall – and results in progressive weakening that can lead to an increased risk for thoracic aortic aneurysm formation and aortic dissection.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Aortic dissection due to Takayasu arteritis (Choice A) is less likely than medial degeneration for this patient as it is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis in large arteries and is most commonly seen in younger females, especially those of Asian ethnicity; it is less likely to occur in a patient in the sixth decade of life with a history of chronic hypertension.

Degeneration of the aortic wall from Marfan syndrome (Choice B) results from a genetic mutation leading to impaired synthesis of collagen. Patients with Marfan syndrome characteristically are diagnosed early in life because of lens dislocation, aneurysmal disease, and joint hypermobility. It can also result in early-onset cystic medial degeneration of the aortic root, which places patients at risk for aortic dissection. Marfan syndrome is less likely the cause of this patient's aortic dissection based on the patient's age and history of hypertension.

Rupture of a sinus of Valsalva aneurysm (Choice D) would result in exsanguination from the aorta into the surrounding aortic adventitia or mediastinum. Sinus of Valsalva aneurysms occur secondary to a number of pathologies, including syphilis, tuberculosis, and chronic cystic medial degeneration. They are less common than aortic dissection as an explanation of the patient’s symptoms.

Traumatic disruption of the aorta from a fall (Choice E) results from shear forces applied to the aorta during rapid deceleration injury such as a fall or high-energy collision. This typically presents with large-volume acute blood loss and hemorrhagic shock.

questionStem: A 27-year-old African American woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of a tight sensation in her chest and a nonproductive cough. The cough occurs most frequently at night after she goes to bed. She says she received breathing treatments in the emergency department for acute shortness of breath twice during the past 3 months and was told to stop smoking. She has a long-standing history of frequent upper respiratory tract infections. She currently takes no medications. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 10 years. Vital signs are within normal limits. End-expiratory wheezes are heard bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?

choices.C: Loss of elastin in the lung matrix

correctExplanation: Asthma is characterized by reversible obstruction to airflow caused by spasm of smooth muscle in the bronchi and small airways. It is often triggered by an allergen. Patients will frequently report worsening of symptoms associated with nighttime, seasonal change, exercise, or exposure to smoke, mold, dust, pollen, or cockroaches. It is diagnosed on clinical history, pulmonary function testing, and/or functional challenge testing (e.g., bronchodilator challenge). Treatment is based on severity and involves avoidance of triggers, the use of short- or long-acting beta-agonists (e.g., albuterol, salmeterol), systemic or inhaled glucocorticoids, anticholinergics, mast cell stabilizers, leukotriene inhibitors, and anti-IgE agents. The exact therapeutic regimen depends on severity and frequency of symptoms. Mast cells produce histamines and leukotrienes in response to activation by allergens, which can trigger bronchial smooth muscle reactivity leading to an exacerbation of asthma.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Embolism of intravascular thrombi (Choice B) describes a pulmonary embolism, often following a deep venous thrombosis, which typically presents with acute onset chest pain, shortness of breath, tachypnea, and tachycardia. This patient is instead showing signs of asthma such as wheezing, nighttime exacerbations, and appropriate response to beta-agonists.

Loss of elastin in the lung matrix (Choice C) describes the pathophysiology of emphysema secondary to chronic inflammation resulting in protease and anti-protease imbalances in the lung, typically from smoking.

Necrotizing pulmonary vasculitis (Choice D) may describe several types of pulmonary vasculitis, for example, Goodpasture syndrome, a vasculitis involving the basement membranes of the lung and kidney, or granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis), a vasculitis involving the upper respiratory mucosa, lungs, and kidneys. Classically, pulmonary vasculitis involves chest pain and hemoptysis, not wheezing.

Noncaseating granulomatous inflammation (Choice E) can occur with several diseases involving the lung, including sarcoidosis and various pneumoconioses. These conditions present with restrictive, not obstructive, lung mechanics.

questionStem: Immediately after an episode of massive hematemesis, a 50-year-old man feels faint, cold, and sweaty. His pulse is 130/min, and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg; hematocrit is 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in patient care?

choices.A: Rapid infusion of 5% dextrose in water
choices.C: Insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter via the subclavian vein
choices.D: Gastric lavage with ice-cold saline until bleeding stops

correctExplanation: Rapid infusion of 0.9% isotonic saline is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's decompensated hemorrhagic shock. In cases of acute blood loss, small amounts can be tolerated without challenging the ability of the circulatory system to compensate. As the amount of blood loss increases, the circulatory system compensates through fluid retention, increased heart rate, and vasoconstriction. If blood loss continues, these mechanisms become incapable of fully compensating, and shock secondary to hemorrhage occurs. Hemorrhagic shock can be classified by the amount of blood lost, vital signs, physiologic parameters such as falling urine output, exam findings such as diaphoresis, cool extremities, and weak peripheral pulses, and features in the history such as light-headedness. In extreme cases, hypotension occurs, necessitating rapid intravascular volume repletion to prevent circulatory collapse, cardiac arrest, and death. In the emergent setting, the patient's acute hypovolemia should be replaced with isotonic saline. In hemorrhage, both red blood cells and plasma are lost equivalently; this results in a normal hematocrit, though overall blood volume is decreased.
incorrectExplanation: Rapid infusion of 5% dextrose in water (Choice A) may be appropriate if normal saline or blood is unavailable, though the osmolality of this fluid results in extravascular losses, making it suboptimal for intravascular volume repletion. Insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter via the subclavian vein (Choice C) is an important diagnostic step in evaluating undifferentiated shock when the cause is not evident from the history and physical exam; this is especially true in the evaluation of cardiogenic shock. This patient demonstrates a clear primary hemorrhagic shock from hematemesis and does not require a pulmonary artery catheter to diagnose or treat at this time. Gastric lavage with ice-cold saline until bleeding stops (Choice D) would not readily replace intravascular volume though it may have an adjunct role in reducing gastrointestinal blood losses; however, emergency esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) (Choice E) is the first choice for definitive hemorrhage control in capable centers. EGD and gastric lavage should not take the place of emergent intravascular volume repletion as the best next step in a patient with decompensated hemorrhagic shock.

questionStem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-month history of progressive shortness of breath and fatigue. She has had no chest pain. There is no history of heart or pulmonary disease. She is in moderate respiratory distress. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention. Crackles are heard halfway up both lungs. A grade 2/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard along the left sternal border. There is an S3. She has 2+ edema of the lower extremities. Rectal examination shows dark stool; test for occult blood is positive. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 5 g/dL, Leukocyte count 9000/mm3, Serum Na+ 140 mEq/L, K+ 4 mEq/L, Cl− 105 mEq/L, HCO3− 25 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, Glucose 120 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, Urine protein 1+. An x-ray of the chest shows a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette with pulmonary vascular congestion. An ECG shows nonspecific ST-segment changes. Echocardiography shows trace mitral regurgitation and an ejection fraction of 70%; there are no wall motion abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Shortness of breath, fatigue, tachycardia, tachypnea, jugular venous distention, bilateral basilar crackles, an S3 gallop, ejection murmur, and lower extremity edema raise suspicion for heart failure, either from a primary consequence of ischemic heart disease, or from a nonischemic cardiomyopathy. In this case, dark stools and a hemoglobin concentration of 5 g/dL indicates the patient suffers from high-output heart failure related to underlying severe anemia; the heart must increase cardiac output through an increase in heart rate and potentially in stroke volume to deliver the same amount of oxygen to the body given diminished oxygen carrying capacity from anemia. Oxygen delivery is a function of cardiac output and oxygen content. If oxygen content falls, cardiac output must rise to maintain equivalent delivery. The oxygen content of blood is directly proportional to the amount of hemoglobin and the saturation of that hemoglobin, and to a much lesser extent, directly proportional to the partial pressure of oxygen in the bloodstream.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (Choice B) is characterized by impaired relaxation and chamber hypertrophy on echocardiography; it typically presents with pulmonary vascular congestion and is often the consequence of chronic, poorly controlled hypertension or aortic stenosis. Left ventricular systolic dysfunction (Choice C) is often the result of ischemic cardiomyopathy but can also result from many nonischemic causes (e.g., alcohol abuse, beriberi, South American trypanosomiasis, chemotherapies, or peripartum cardiomyopathy). It typically presents with a reduced ejection fraction and is seen on echocardiography as an enlarged, dilated chamber with poor contractility. Nephrotic syndrome (Choice D) presents with edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hypercoagulability, and increased susceptibility to infection. This patient's symptoms are more likely explained by heart failure secondary to anemia as opposed to a primary renal process. Valvular heart disease (Choice E) is a common cause of heart failure; however, this patient has no significant valvular dysfunction on echocardiography.

questionStem: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of abdominal bloating, increasing flatulence, and diarrhea 6 to 12 times daily despite loperamide therapy. The stool is watery, nonbloody, and foul smelling; he says it is bright yellow and occasionally green. He has not had fever. He recently traveled to the Middle East. His temperature is 37°C(98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows slight distention and mild tenderness with no rebound or guarding; bowel sounds are normal. Rectal examination shows no abnormalities. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) is the most common cause of travelers’ diarrhea. It is one of the most common causes of bacterial diarrhea in the developing world and is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. Symptoms include acute, diffuse, crampy abdominal pain and bloating, and profuse, frequent episodes of watery, nonbloody diarrhea. ETEC causes diarrhea through the production of bacterial exotoxins. Diagnosis is via stool culture and microscopy (typically with an absence of blood and stool leukocytes), and treatment is supportive with rehydration and electrolyte repletion. The infection is often self-limiting, though antibiotics may be required in prolonged or severe cases.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, F, G, H, I, and J.

Campylobacter jejuni (Choice A), Entamoeba histolytica (Choice D), nontyphoidal Salmonella species (Choice F), Shigella species (Choice I), and Yersinia enterocolitica (Choice J) classically present with mucosal inflammation and invasion, leading to a toxic presentation with bloody diarrhea. Clostridium difficile (Choice B), can present with watery or bloody diarrhea depending on the severity of the infection and often follows antibiotic administration. These pathogens are invasive, toxin-producing, and require antibiotic therapy plus supportive care.

Entamoeba coli (Choice C) is a commensal organism that generally does not cause pathologic enteritis or colitis.

Norwalk virus (Choice G) is a cause of self-limited viral gastroenteritis with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. It is commonly detected in outbreaks on cruise ships and commonly occurs during winter months.

Rotavirus (Choice H) causes self-limited nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhea in children, with nearly 100% of children having been affected by age five.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman has had polyuria, blurred vision, and rapid breathing for 1 day. Her pulse is 110/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 100/50 mm Hg. Examination is otherwise within normal limits. Serum studies show: Na+ 139 mEq/L, Cl- 99 mEq/L, K+ 4.7 mEq/L, HCO3- 18 mEq/L, Glucose 783 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her acidosis?

choices.D: Loss of bicarbonate through the kidneys
choices.E: Movement of potassium into the cells

correctExplanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) occurs due to the accumulation of serum ketones such as β-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs because of the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Patients present with fatigue, polyuria, shortness of breath, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Vital signs may show tachycardia and tachypnea. Kussmaul respirations, rapid and deep, is a classic physical exam finding because of respiratory compensation for the underlying metabolic acidosis. Labs typically show increased glucose, ketones, and a high anion-gap because of the accumulation of unmeasured anions in serum. Anion gap is calculated as the difference between sodium and the sum of bicarbonate and chloride anions. Treatment is through replacement of insulin, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions.
incorrectExplanation: Accumulation of lactate (Choice B), also known as lactic acidosis, can occur in multiple different situations such as shock, metabolic derangements, and in response to medications. It can also occur in DKA; however, it is not the primary cause of acidosis. Decreased renal production of ammonium (Choice C) and loss of bicarbonate through the kidneys (Choice D) are both causes of renal tubular acidosis (RTA). RTAs are not caused by the accumulation of an unmeasured anion and do not present with an increased anion gap. Movement of potassium into the cells (Choice E) occurs because of transcellular potassium-proton exchange. Increased movement of potassium into the cells occurs when the serum is alkalotic, not acidotic. Acidosis in the setting of DKA stimulates movement of potassium out of the cells into the serum.

questionStem: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-hour history of muscle swelling and tenderness of the left thigh following minimal trauma. He has severe hemophilia A and has received factor VIII replacement therapy for bleeding episodes since childhood. Over recent months, his bleeding has been poorly controlled; increasing doses of factor VIII have been required to stop bleeding episodes. His platelet count is 125,000/mm³, and activated partial thromboplastin time is greater than 120 sec. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis of this patient's increased bleeding?

choices.C: Measurement of thrombin time to detect heparin

correctExplanation: Hemophilia A, an X-linked coagulopathy, arises from a genetic deficiency in factor VIII synthesis or activity. Patients often present with easy bruising and hemorrhage involving muscles and joints. Hemorrhage can be life-threatening, often requiring transfusions of factor VIII to replace the deficient protein. Patients can acquire antibodies against exogenous factor VIII, which can necessitate larger transfusions to elicit the same hemostatic effect. With an acquired inhibitor, some of the transfused factor VIII will be bound and neutralized by the inhibitor (typically IgG). Testing for factor VIII inhibitor is indicated in such cases. Exposure to the nonnative protein (transfused factor VIII) promotes this appropriate but countertherapeutic immune response.
incorrectExplanation: Bleeding time (Choice A) is a measure of platelet function and is used in the diagnosis of platelet disorders such as thrombocytopenia, von Willebrand disease, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, and Glanzmann thrombasthenia. It does not classically have a role in the workup of hemophilia and does not correlate with coagulation factor deficiencies. Measurement of factor IX concentration (Choice B) is useful in the workup of hemophilia B. This patient has hemophilia A and is presenting with symptoms concerning for the development of an acquired inhibitor of factor VIII. The presence of both hemophilia A and hemophilia B in the same patient is exceedingly rare. Measurement of thrombin time to detect heparin (Choice C) would be appropriate if the patient were using heparin therapeutically. Platelet function tests (Choice D) refer to bleeding time, platelet aggregation, and platelet activation tests. They are classically used to assess qualitative platelet hemostatic defects. This patient presents with a known factor deficiency and progressive under-responsiveness to an exogenously replaced protein, raising suspicion for the presence of an acquired factor inhibitor.

questionStem: A 23-year-old African American man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of increasing pain and swelling above the right knee. There is no history of trauma or recent fever. He had retinoblastoma in infancy that was treated with enucleation. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows moderate swelling of the distal femur. There is mild tenderness to palpation with moderate discomfort on weight bearing. His serum alkaline phosphatase activity is 1350 U/L. An x-ray of the right femur shows a lytic lesion with periosteal new bone at the margins. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Chronic pain, bony swelling, and a history of malignancy in childhood raises suspicion for a diagnosis of osteosarcoma, the most common type of primary bone cancer. It often occurs in persons under age 30 years. Osteosarcoma typically occurs in long bones, frequently above the knee in the distal femur or below the knee in the proximal tibia. The metaphysis is often affected. The initial presentation often includes pain and swelling; sometimes, a fragility fracture is the declaring presentation. Causes include familial cases, especially involving the retinoblastoma or p53 tumor suppressor genes, bony dysplasia such as osteitis deformans (Paget disease) and fibrous dysplasia, and exposure to radiation. Diagnosis occurs via a bone biopsy and is supported by radiographic findings, such as the Codman triangle (an area of reactive periosteum adjacent to a lytic lesion with new bone formation).
incorrectExplanation: Hyperparathyroidism (Choice A) presents with bony destruction caused by hyperactive osteoclast activity, known as osteitis fibrosa cystica. It is typically diffuse and is also accompanied by symptoms of hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia. Metastatic malignancy (Choice B) is the most common overall source of bone tumors, secondary to spread from a primary malignancy (often lung or prostate). Metastatic lesions would be unlikely to occur in an otherwise healthy young person and would be less likely to present with a localized lesion at the metaphysis of a long bone. Multiple myeloma (Choice C) presents with multiple areas of bony osteolysis and remodeling, caused by local invasive disease and its effect on increased osteoclast activity. Lesions are often in the skull, pelvis, or vertebrae, and often occur in patients in their sixth or greater decades of life. Symptoms also include anemia, renal failure, frequent infections, and diffuse skeletal pain. It would be rare in a young person with an isolated tumor. Osteitis deformans (Paget disease) (Choice D) presents with breakdown, remodeling, and disorganized deposition of new bone, and results in deformity, pain, fragility fractures, and arthritis. It is rare in youth. Osteoid osteomas (Choice E) are benign tumors often occurring most often in the long bones of children and young adults; they tend to be self-limited and cause pain, especially at nighttime. They are generally small and do not have a strong association with tumor suppressor genes. Osteomyelitis (Choice F) is an infection of bone and bone marrow and typically presents acutely, subacutely, or chronically from direct inoculation or hematogenous spread; patients typically describe symptoms of pain, difficulty bearing weight, and overlying erythema. Imaging typically demonstrates localized osseous erosive changes. Osteoporosis (Choice G) occurs in older persons, often female, because of loss of bone density with age. It does not have a lytic appearance or periosteal reaction on imaging. Sickle cell disease (Choice I) can cause bone infarction and avascular necrosis during occlusive crises, though this patient has no history of the condition. It would not present with a tumor or periosteal reaction.

questionStem: A previously healthy 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department 2 weeks after the onset of mild cough and runny nose. During the past 3 days, the cough has worsened with episodes so intense that he has vomited. The cough is productive of thick green sputum. He feels well between coughing episodes. He has not had fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath. He takes no medications. He is a college student. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 115/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Pulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Episodes of severe coughing followed by emesis, in the setting of a respiratory illness, raises suspicion for pertussis. Pertussis is caused by infection from Bordetella pertussis and classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, which presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after 1 to 2 weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, at times violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, and pneumothoraces. Often, such coughing fits are followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months. Symptoms resolve in the convalescent stage, which lasts from 1 to 4 weeks. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization, and is treated with antibiotics, typically macrolides.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Influenza (Choice A) presents with respiratory, gastrointestinal, and systemic symptoms, including cough, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, chills, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias; it can be complicated by bacterial superinfection causing severe bacterial pneumonia. It typically lasts for less than 1 week and does not have a paroxysmal stage.

Legionnaires disease (Choice B) is caused by infection from Legionella pneumophila, which is typically spread through aerosol transmission from a water habitat source (e.g., air conditioning). It often presents with diarrhea and hyponatremia in addition to respiratory symptoms and does not typically have a paroxysmal stage.

Psittacosis (Choice D) occurs in persons with exposure to birds, as a vector is typically required to transmit the infection (Chlamydia psittaci); similarly, Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) (Choice E) typically requires exposure to sheep, goats, and cattle as a zoonotic source.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman who is HIV positive comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of fever, shortness of breath, right-sided chest pain, and cough productive of yellow-brown sputum. She had previously been feeling well. She is compliant with her antiretroviral medication regimen and follow-up visits. One month ago, her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 400/mm3 (Normal:>500), and plasma HIV viral load was undetectable. She has never used illicit drugs. Her temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 90/40 mm Hg. Bronchial breath sounds and egophony are heard over the lower lobe of the right lung posteriorly; there is dullness to percussion. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. An x-ray of the chest shows a right lower lobe consolidation. A Gram stain of sputum shows many segmented neutrophils and numerous gram-positive diplococci. Cultures of the sputum and blood are pending. In addition to supplemental oxygen and intravenous fluids, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Fever, shortness of breath, cough productive of yellow-brown sputum, focal pleuritic chest pain, toxic vital signs, and a consolidation on chest x-ray are suggestive of lobar pneumonia, often from S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, or S. aureus (especially if preceded by a viral infection). S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus and can be treated using an anti-pneumococcal beta-lactam antibiotic such as ceftriaxone. This patient, while HIV-positive, has acceptable levels of CD4+ T-lymphocytes and an undetectable HIV viral load. She has had no recent hospitalizations and is adherent to her HIV medication regimen. Given her well-controlled disease, she does not require broader spectrum antibiotics or antibiotic prophylaxis at this time.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, E, and F.

Gentamicin (Choice B), an aminoglycoside antibiotic, is commonly used to treat neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and pneumonia, pelvic inflammatory disease, endocarditis, and osteomyelitis; however, it is ototoxic, nephrotoxic, and neurotoxic, making it suboptimal when alternative suitable and safer medications are available.

Isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide (Choice C) is an appropriate combination of antibiotics for infections caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Penicillin (Choice D) is a beta-lactam antibiotic, but resistance rates for S. pneumoniae are high, making it less suitable for empiric antibiotic therapy.

Prednisone (Choice E) has an adjunct role in treating pulmonary infections; however, in a patient without chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or pneumonia suspected to be from P. jirovecii, a glucocorticoid is not typically indicated and an antibiotic is the most appropriate next therapy.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Choice F) is commonly used in HIV patients as prophylaxis against P. jirovecii pneumonia when the CD4+ count falls below 200/mm3. It is not first-line antibiotic for suspected lobar pneumonia from S. pneumoniae.

questionStem: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at a restaurant. Her pulse is 120/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Her breathing is labored, but she can speak. She has diffuse bronchospasm, and she coughs continuously. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Anaphylactic shock, a severe Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction, presents following exposure to an allergen. It is caused by widespread IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and is characterized by histaminergic responses within multiple organ systems leading to flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and vasodilation, which can lead to airway obstruction and circulatory collapse. If not managed promptly, death can occur from hypoxia and/or distributive shock. The diagnosis is made clinically, and treatment requires intramuscular epinephrine, inhaled beta-agonists, glucocorticoids, histamine blockers, fluid resuscitation, and potentially invasive airway or additional vasopressor support.
incorrectExplanation:
Aspiration (Choice B), the inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents into the airway, occurs because of dysfunction in the swallowing mechanism, commonly from anatomic (e.g., malignancy, tracheoesophageal fistula), neurologic (e.g., post-stroke with cranial nerve dysfunction or impaired swallow coordination, emesis occurring when unconscious and unable to protect airway), or functional mechanisms (e.g., cyclic vomiting, frequent emesis in alcohol use disorder). It classically presents with cough and shortness of breath but would not be expected to result in acute onset tachycardia and hypotension unless a massive volume aspiration took place.

Drug overdose (Choice C) can result in respiratory distress, but more often results in shallow and depressed respirations (opioid overdose), or tachypnea (stimulant overdose). Bronchospasm would be unlikely.

Pulmonary embolus (Choice D) presents with acute onset chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia, often in a patient with a history of deep venous thrombosis. The lungs are characteristically clear to auscultation early in the course.

Spontaneous pneumothorax (Choice E) presents with chest pain and tachypnea with diminished breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion on the affected side; it can present with shock in the setting of a tension pneumothorax. Bronchospasm is less likely.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has a 5-year history of mild shortness of breath on exertion and cough productive of copious yellow-to-whitish sputum. She has not had fever or chills. She has reactive airways disease treated with daily salmeterol-fluticasone and albuterol and seasonal allergies treated with fexofenadine. She has a chronic cough that is not controlled by her medications. She has a 20-year history of multiple respiratory tract infections, including three episodes of pneumonia during the past 15 years and two episodes of sinusitis during the past 5 years. She usually requires antibiotic therapy for bronchitis three to four times yearly. She does not smoke. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Examination shows mild lymphadenopathy. There is mild thrush. Coarse breath sounds are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities except for a slightly increased S2. There is no clubbing or edema. In addition to pulmonary function testing and antifungal therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: A history of multiple sinopulmonary infections in an otherwise healthy adult along with thrush raises the possibility of a late-presenting primary immunodeficiency, in this case, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). CVID classically presents in the second to fourth decades of life as multiple, recurrent sinus or pulmonary infections, including pneumonia, bronchitis, and sinusitis. An opportunistic infection like thrush, while potentially related to the patient's use of inhaled corticosteroids, further raises the possibility of an immunodeficiency. The patient should be tested for serum immunoglobulin concentrations.
incorrectExplanation: Measurement of CD4+ T-lymphocyte count (Choice A) would be appropriate in the case of known or suspected infection with HIV or AIDS. This patient has no clear risk factors for HIV/AIDS, and her infections are more likely explained by CVID. Measurement of serum complement concentrations (Choice B) would be appropriate if an innate immunodeficiency related to complement were suspected; notably, susceptibility to infection from Neisseria species is associated with deficiencies in the terminal complement proteins C5-C9. Sputum culture (Choice D) would be appropriate in cases where gram stain or culture of an organism would improve diagnostic or therapeutic ability in the management of a pulmonary infection, though sputum culture is often difficult to obtain in nonintubated patients and may be confounded by oral and native respiratory flora. It would not explain her recurrent infections over many years. Ventilation-perfusion lung scans (Choice E) are used in the diagnosis of conditions that affect either pulmonary ventilation or perfusion, notably pulmonary embolism.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of dizziness and progressive difficulty with balance. She has been supporting herself against walls when she walks. She has not had numbness, weakness, or palpitations. She has had nausea and a mild decrease in appetite but is able to drink fluids. There is no history of head trauma. She has mitral valve prolapse. She takes no medications. Her sister has multiple sclerosis. Vital signs are within normal limits. The optic discs appear normal, and ocular movements are full. Tympanic membranes are dull bilaterally. The light reflex is distorted. There are no exudates on the pharynx. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard best at the lower left sternal border. Muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes are normal. Her gait is unsteady. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Dizziness and gait instability carry a broad differential diagnosis; these symptoms are often divided into central, peripheral, and secondary causes of symptoms to determine a likely diagnosis. Central causes include cerebrovascular accidents such as ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes, tumors of the brain stem and cerebellum, and multiple sclerosis or similar demyelinating disorders. Peripheral causes include benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, labyrinthitis, Meniere disease, endolymphatic fistula, or temporal bone fractures, tumors, or lesions. Secondary or systemic causes can include electrolyte imbalances, hypovolemia, cardiac arrhythmia, infections, and vitamin deficiencies, among other causes. Labyrinthitis is inflammation of the inner ear, often involving the vestibulocochlear nerve, and is often preceded by an upper respiratory or ear infection. Classic symptoms include vertigo, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, and hearing loss. Treatment is supportive, along with the exclusion of emergent causes of vertigo and ataxia, as the condition is typically self-limited.
incorrectExplanation:
Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) (Choice A) is a known cause of central vertigo secondary to impingement of the vestibulocochlear nerve at the brain stem. These tumors often occur at the cerebellopontine angle and are often subclinical; there is an association with neurofibromatosis, and they may present with hearing loss, vertigo, and nystagmus. Preceding infection or dulling of the tympanic membranes would not be expected.

Cerebral infarction (Choice B) can cause vertigo by disrupting normal neurologic equilibrium and proprioceptive pathways, especially when such infarction involves the cerebellum, pons, or brain stem nuclei involving the oculomotor, trochlear, abducens, or vestibulocochlear nerves. Nystagmus, motor or sensory neurologic deficits, and cranial nerve deficits would be expected in such cases, and the presentation is typically acute. Signs of vertebrobasilar insufficiency, such as nausea, vomiting, dysarthria, and impaired brain stem reflexes may also be present.

Dehydration (Choice C) may present with dizziness or ataxia in the setting of orthostatic hypotension, with patients often describing feelings of light-headedness when rising from supine to seated or seated to standing. It is caused by decreased cardiac output from diminished preload and resolves with volume resuscitation.

Endocarditis (Choice D) presents with acute or subacute fever, a new or changing heart murmur, septic emboli to the lung or systemic circulation, and vascular and immunologic phenomena such as Roth spots, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, and splinter hemorrhages.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) (Choice F) presents with neurologic symptoms of varying duration separated in space and time. Common symptoms include optic neuritis, which is often the declaring presentation. Women are more commonly affected than men. Any type of neurologic symptom may occur. MS would not be expected to follow an infection though it may be exacerbated by such, and physical exam findings of tympanic membrane dullness (suggestive of inflammation and fluid in the middle ear) would not be present.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician with his wife because of a headache for 3 days. He has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain over the past 6 months. His dentist has told him that the space between his teeth is increasing. His wife says that he has started snoring and his voice has deepened over the past 6 months. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and now weighs 91 kg (200 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m2. Examination shows frontal bossing and large feet. Measurement of which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Acromegaly results from excess production of growth hormone (GH), typically from a functional pituitary adenoma. GH upregulates production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). Following fusion of growth plates, stimulus from IGF-1 results in enlargement of bones in the head, face, hands, and feet, sparing the long bones. If the derangement occurs prior to puberty, long-bone enlargement also occurs, resulting in gigantism. Symptoms of acromegaly include the development of enlarged hands, feet, forehead, skull, and jaw, and deepening of the voice. Complications include the development of diabetes mellitus. Diagnosis is made by clinical presentation, measured hormonal levels, and cross-sectional imaging to detect the culprit adenoma. Surgical resection is the preferred treatment. If surgery cannot be performed, somatostatin analogues (e.g., octreotide) and antagonists of the GH receptor (e.g., pegvisomant) can be used.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Hemoglobin A1c (Choice A) is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus when increased above 6.5%. It results from chronic elevations in blood glucose leading to the production of glycated hemoglobin and can be used for the diagnosis and assessment of treatment efficacy for diabetes mellitus. It has no role in the immediate diagnosis of acromegaly.

Serum C-peptide concentration (Choice B) is also used in the diagnosis of diabetes and can be useful in distinguishing whether the cause is due to beta cell destruction (insulin and C-peptide concentration will both be low, type 1 diabetes mellitus) or decreased insulin sensitivity (insulin and C-peptide concentration will both be increased, type 2 diabetes mellitus). It can also be used in diagnosing factitious hypoglycemia, when a patient may be suspected of self-administering insulin; resultant negative feedback on the pancreas will decrease production of native insulin and C-peptide in this scenario.

Serum growth hormone-releasing hormone concentration (Choice C) could be useful if a hypothalamic cause was suspected for acromegaly; a pituitary adenoma with resultant loss of normal feedback mechanisms is more common.

Serum somatostatin concentration (Choice E) does not play a role in the diagnosis of acromegaly; rather, somatostatin analogues can be used in the treatment of the condition.

questionStem: A previously healthy 72-year-old man who is a retired shipyard worker comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of nonproductive cough and shortness of breath. He does not smoke. Breath sounds are decreased, and there is dullness to percussion at the left lung base. An x-ray of the chest shows calcified pleural plaques and a left pleural effusion. A thoracentesis is performed, and analysis of the pleural fluid shows a glucose concentration of 4 mg/dL. The most likely underlying cause of these findings is exposure to which of the following?
correctExplanation: A history of working in a shipyard, chronic cough, shortness of breath, and pleural effusion plus calcified pleural plaques on x-ray raises suspicion for malignant mesothelioma. Exposure to asbestos in the shipyard is a known risk factor. Pleural fluid analysis is indicated to characterize the underlying cause, as markers in the pleural fluid can narrow the diagnosis by investigating infection, malignancy, inflammation, and transudative causes of effusion. Pleural fluid pH and glucose are markers of cell metabolism; a low pleural fluid glucose indicates increased cell metabolism and is a negative prognostic indicator in malignant mesothelioma.
incorrectExplanation:
Exposure to graphite (Choice B) dust has been associated with pneumoconiosis, a cause of restrictive lung disease in the form of pulmonary fibrosis.

Isocyanate exposure (Choice C) occurs from industrial application of paints, varnishes, and foams; exposure has been associated with many pulmonary diseases including hypersensitivity pneumonitis, bronchitis, interstitial pneumonia, asthma, emphysema, and pulmonary edema. Isocyanates are not commonly associated with malignant mesothelioma.

Mycobacterium kansasii (Choice D) causes chronic pulmonary infection that resembles tuberculosis, presenting with fever, cough, night sweats, and weight loss, often in patients with immunocompromised states. It would not likely present with pleural plaques following years of working in a shipyard.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae (Choice E) is a common cause of atypical pneumonia, and presents with acute cough, fever, chills, and shortness of breath. The chest x-ray would typically demonstrate multifocal infiltrates without pleural plaques.

Nocardia asteroides (Choice F) causes nocardiosis, which presents as pulmonary or disseminated infection, often in patients who are immunocompromised. The pulmonary variant presents with fever, night sweats, cough, and weight loss, and chest x-ray demonstrates multifocal infiltrates, often with necrosis.

Household dwellers exposed to radon (Choice G) are at risk for malignancy. Exposure typically occurs in the home, especially the basement, in geographic regions of prevalence. Radon diffuses into air within basements and homes, where it is inhaled. The decay products are radioactive, which promotes mutations leading to the development of bronchogenic lung cancer, not mesothelioma.

Exposure to silicon (Choice H), similar to graphite, leads to pneumoconiosis, characterized by restrictive lung disease and pulmonary fibrosis.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of shortness of breath and wheezing for 2 days. He has had swelling of the lower legs since he returned from a 200-mile car trip 3 days ago. He has a 20-year history of poorly controlled hypertension currently treated with hydrochlorothiazide. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min and regular, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention. Crackles and wheezes are heard in the lower lung fields bilaterally. A prominent S3 gallop is heard at the apex. There is 4+ ankle edema. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly and cephalization of the pulmonary vessels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Shortness of breath, edema, jugular venous distention (JVD), crackles in dependent areas of lung, a history of poorly controlled hypertension, tachypnea, tachycardia, and an x-ray showing cardiomegaly with cephalization of vessels raises suspicion for cardiogenic pulmonary edema because of increased pressures in the left side of the heart, pulmonary veins, and pulmonary capillaries. Pulmonary edema can also occur from non-cardiogenic sources (e.g., acute respiratory distress syndrome, multifocal pneumonia, burns/inhalation injuries, high altitude, and drowning). Because of increased left-heart filling pressures in heart failure, the pulmonary venous pressure rises, which in turn results in increased pressures in pulmonary capillaries. This increased hydrostatic pressure results in interstitial edema and eventually alveolar edema. This is seen clinically as shortness of breath and respiratory distress and is supported by signs of hypervolemia such as peripheral edema, JVD, S3 gallop, and crackles on lung examination. Vital signs typically show tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Treatment is through diuretics to reduce the patient’s hypervolemic state and lower cardiac filling pressure, pulmonary venous, and pulmonary capillary pressure. Nitroglycerin, a venodilator, can also be utilized to shift fluid into capacitance vessels and lower preload. Positive pressure ventilation can also reduce alveolar and interstitial edema and drive fluid back into circulation.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and F.

Aspiration pneumonia (Choice A) presents as shortness of breath, cough productive of sputum, and fever, with a focal consolidation on chest x-ray, often in the superior segment of the inferior right lobe of lung. This is the most common location for an aspiration event to occur when a patient is supine. An aspiration event must be in the history to diagnose aspiration pneumonia; thus, the patient will often have a history of swallowing dysfunction, stroke, oropharyngeal or laryngeal malignancy, or a condition that causes frequent vomiting and retching such as alcoholism or bulimia.

Bronchiectasis (Choice B) presents with signs of obstructive lung disease, and often follows chronic pulmonary necrotizing infections, which can occur in the setting of cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Patients will present with wheezing and mucus plugging, and unless concomitant right heart failure is present, would not necessarily present with signs of hypervolemia (e.g., edema, JVD). Cephalization of vessels would also be atypical, unless left heart failure were also present. Chest x-ray often shows marked bronchial dilatation and wall thickening.

Chronic bronchitis (Choice C) presents with chronic productive cough and signs of obstructive lung disease (e.g., wheezing, air trapping). It often occurs in smokers as a component of the spectrum of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, in tandem with emphysema. This commonly results in right heart failure from chronic hypoxemic pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction. This would potentially manifest with JVD, ascites, and lower extremity edema, less likely pulmonary edema.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Choice D) is caused by an exaggerated immune response (typically type 3 or type 4 hypersensitivity) to an inhaled antigen. It can present in acute, subacute, or chronic forms, with the acute form characterized by shortness of breath, cough, and systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, headache, and rash, following exposure to an antigen. The chest x-ray may be normal at this stage or may show interstitial infiltrates. The subacute and chronic forms commonly present with dyspnea, cough, fatigue, and weight loss. Imaging reveals interstitial inflammation and fibrosis of the lung. Pulmonary function tests generally demonstrate a restrictive pattern. Unless concomitant heart failure were present, signs of volume overload and cephalization of the vessels would be unlikely.

Pulmonary embolism (Choice F) is characteristically associated with long periods of immobilization such as orthopaedic surgery, intensive care unit stay, long drives, and long plane flights, because of the association with deep venous thrombosis (DVT) formation from venous stasis. DVT classically presents with unilateral lower extremity edema, and when an embolus travels to the lung, the patient may become symptomatic. Classic symptoms include rapid-onset chest pain and dyspnea; if an infarction has occurred, pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis may be present. Vital signs are often notable for tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia; hypotension can be present if the embolus is large enough to obstruct blood flow from the right heart. The lungs are typically clear to auscultation, and cardiomegaly and cephalization of the vessels would be unlikely unless concomitant heart failure were present.

questionStem: A previously healthy 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of fever, chills, and left flank pain. She also has had nausea and vomited four times during this period. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft with tenderness to percussion over the left flank. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 39%, Leukocyte count 22,000/mm³, Urine RBC 10–20/hpf, WBC 20–50/hpf. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Fever, chills, left flank pain, nausea, and vomiting raises suspicion for pyelonephritis, an infection of the kidney that commonly results from retrograde spread of a urinary tract infection. Urinary tract infections are much more common in women due to the shorter urethra and favorable regional environment for bacterial growth. If untreated, bacteria can travel up the ureter to infect the kidney, resulting in pyelonephritis. Lower urinary tract infection symptoms include dysuria, frequency, urgency, incontinence, and suprapubic pain. Systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, nausea, and vomiting are less likely, and vital signs are often normal. Urine may be dark colored or foul smelling. Upper urinary tract infections more commonly occur with systemic symptoms such as rigors, nausea, vomiting, myalgias, arthralgias, and fatigue; patients with pyelonephritis often present with high fevers, tachycardia, leukocytosis, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness on physical examination. Severe infections can be accompanied by hypotension. Urinalysis in pyelonephritis often shows greater than 10 leukocytes per high power field, may show red cells as evidence of mucosal inflammation (or concomitant nephrolithiasis), and may show white blood cell casts. Bacteria are generally seen on microscopy, with gram-negative rods being the most common pathogen. An antibiotic with sufficient broad coverage of gram-negative rods should be chosen, such as intravenous ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Oral or intravenous amoxicillin (Choices A and C) generally covers gram-positive bacteria, with limited coverage of gram-negative bacteria unless paired with a beta-lactamase inhibitor such as clavulanic acid. Oral azithromycin (Choice B) is generally ineffective in treating urinary tract infections as it has limited spectrum against gram-negative pathogens; it is also primarily excreted hepatically and has not been shown to concentrate in urine. It is much more commonly used in sinusitis, pharyngitis, respiratory, and sexually transmitted infections. Intravenous metronidazole (Choice E) is used primarily to treat anaerobic bacterial and parasitic infections such as Clostridium difficile and infections caused by the Giardia, Clostridia, Gardnerella, and Trichinella species; and amoebic infections. Intravenous metronidazole does not have a primary role in treating pyelonephritis or urinary tract infections.

questionStem: A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of swelling of her face and legs for 2 weeks. As the day progresses, her facial swelling resolves, but her legs become increasingly swollen. Her pulse is 64/min and regular, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. There is 1+ presacral edema and 2+ edema of the lower extremities. Her prothrombin time is 12 seconds (INR=1.1), and serum albumin concentration is 2.3 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's edema?
correctExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure. This occurs because of loss of normal size and charge filtration of the glomerular capillary and Bowman's capsule interface. Causes of nephrotic syndrome include minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, and focal segmental glomerular sclerosis. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs; foamy or dark-colored urine; hypoalbuminemia; and proteinuria. Complications include hypercoagulability caused by urinary loss of antithrombin-3 and infection caused by urinary loss of gamma globulins. Workup includes renal biopsy and treating underlying causes such as HIV, hepatitis, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Treatment involves the use of glucocorticoids and immunomodulators, though treatment-refractory disease is common. Patients may ultimately require renal replacement therapy or transplantation.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, I, J, K, and L.

Cellulitis (Choice A) presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, and induration, often following inoculation from an injury such as an abrasion. It is typically localized and would not present with diffuse dependent edema or hypoalbuminemia.

Cirrhosis (Choice B) can present with edema caused by loss of oncotic pressure, though it also presents with ascites, increased bilirubin, jaundice, and signs of portal hypertension such as esophageal varices, splenomegaly, caput medusae, and rectal varices. It typically occurs in patients with preceding conditions such as alcohol abuse or chronic hepatitis.

Congestive heart failure (Choice C) presents with edema caused by increased hydrostatic pressure rather than loss of oncotic pressure.

Deep venous thrombosis (Choice D) is a common cause of lower extremity edema, though it is often unilateral unless the thrombus is large and proximal or bilateral. It would not be expected to cause facial edema or hypoalbuminemia.

Lymphangitis (Choice E) occurs because of infection or inflammation traveling within the lymphatic system and presents with streaking, sometimes traveling away from areas of cellulitis or abscess. It does not generally cause diffuse edema or hypoalbuminemia.

Lymphedema (Choice F) occurs because of obstruction or excision of lymphatic channels, such as in cases of lymphoma or after lymph node dissection. It is typically localized to a single upper, single lower, or bilateral lower extremities, and would not be expected to cause hypoalbuminemia.

Malnutrition (Choice G) can result in edema because of insufficient dietary protein and resultant impaired synthesis of albumin, as seen in Kwashiorkor syndrome. Kwashiorkor is rare in the developed world and would be noted on exam with signs of malnutrition and muscle loss such as temporal wasting and sunken eyes.

Postphlebitic syndrome (Choice I) is characterized by chronic edema following thrombosis. It occurs in an extremity because of valvular insufficiency and chronic venous hypertension following damage from a deep venous thrombosis.

Pulmonary hypertension (Choice J) can be primary (eg, genetic mutation causing smooth muscle hypertrophy and increased pulmonary vascular resistance) or secondary (eg, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic venous thromboembolic disease, pulmonary fibrosis, or heart failure). It presents with signs of right-sided heart failure including dependent edema, jugular venous distention, and hepatic congestion. Examination typically reveals a loud P2, right ventricular heave, and tricuspid regurgitation murmur.

Stasis dermatitis (Choice K) is a chronic inflammatory condition of the skin caused by chronic venous insufficiency. It presents with erythema, scaling, and pruritus of the lower extremities, often with associated edema. It is not associated with hypoalbuminemia.

Varicose veins (Choice L) are dilated superficial veins caused by valvular incompetence. They can cause localized edema and discomfort but are not associated with hypoalbuminemia.
