The patient demonstrates an increased systolic blood pressure of 160 mm Hg and pulse pressure of 74 mm Hg. The patient's diastolic blood pressure of 86 mm Hg is at the upper limit of normal. Increased pulse pressure can occur in the setting of various pathologies, including aortic regurgitation, obstructive sleep apnea, hyperthyroidism, and decreased aortic compliance. Vascular compliance refers to the association between changes in blood volume and pressure, with a decreased compliance resulting in abnormally increased pressure relative to changes in volume. Atherosclerotic calcifications of the thoracic aorta result in decreased aortic compliance and are commonly associated with modifiable risk factors such as hyperlipidemia, smoking, and diabetes mellitus, along with nonmodifiable risk factors such as male sex and increased age. This decreased aortic compliance results in hypertension primarily with isolated systolic blood pressure elevation and is commonly seen in older persons.
incorrectExplanation: Decreased diameter of the vascular lumen (Choice A) would result in increased systemic vascular resistance, most commonly associated with cholesterol atheroma buildup (atherosclerosis) resulting in increased intimal thickening of the arteries (Choice E), especially the arterioles. Decreased vascular lumen diameter would also be seen with increased deposition of lipids in the arterial smooth muscle (Choice C). These would result primarily in an elevation of diastolic blood pressure. Increased deposition of lipofuscin in cardiac myocytes (Choice D) is associated with normal aging and would not directly result in progressive hypertension unless concomitant heart failure was also present.

questionStem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She feels well and has no history of serious illness. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 5 years and drinks two beers daily. She has a sedentary lifestyle. Her mother underwent bilateral knee replacement at the age of 55 years for severe osteoarthritis. The patient is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 101 kg (223 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m². Her pulse is 64/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. She requests advice about how to prevent osteoarthritis. Which of the following is most likely to decrease this patient's risk for osteoarthritis?

choices.E: Estrogen replacement therapy at the onset of menopause

correctExplanation: Weight loss is the most likely modifiable risk factor to decrease this patient's risk for osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis is a noninflammatory arthropathy secondary to deterioration of articular cartilage, often related to multifactorial causes with an interplay of systemic and local factors. Obesity, defined as a body mass index greater than 30 kg/m², is one of the most common risk factors for the development of osteoarthritis. Excess weight results in consistent, increased daily joint stress and degradation of the articular cartilage. Further, humoral factors from adipose cells plus leptin system derangements cause alterations in metabolism of articular cartilage. These factors result in an increased rate of degradation.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Abstinence from alcohol (Choice A) does not directly affect the risk for developing osteoarthritis. Excessive consumption of alcohol does increase the risk for osteoporosis and increases the risk for a patient to become overweight or obese, but it does not itself increase osteoarthritis risk.

Regular aerobic exercise (Choice B) does not demonstrate supporting evidence of increased osteoarthritis risk when performed at light to moderate activity levels and with normal joints. While it can indirectly result in decreased osteoarthritis risk through improved fitness levels and weight loss, it does not directly decrease the risk for osteoarthritis.

Calcium supplementation (Choice D) and estrogen replacement therapy at the onset of menopause (Choice E) would assist in decreasing the risk for osseous demineralization and osteoporosis development but would not play a role in decreasing the risk for osteoarthritis.

questionStem: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of worsening headache and left-sided weakness 1 hour ago. He has no history of serious illness and has not seen a physician for 10 years. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years and drinks six beers daily. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 97 kg (215 lb); BMI is 30 kg/m². His pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 180/120 mm Hg. Examination shows mild-to-moderate weakness of the left lower aspect of the face. Muscle strength is decreased in the left upper and left lower extremities. Funduscopic examination shows an arteriovenous ratio of 1:3 and regions of mild focal spasm of some arterioles. Results of a complete blood count, platelet count, and coagulation studies are within the reference ranges. His serum total cholesterol concentration is 400 mg/dL. A CT scan of the head shows a 1.5 × 2-cm region of hyperintensity centered at the right putamen; there is mild surrounding lucency. Which of the following is most likely to decrease this patient's risk for a recurrent stroke of this type?
correctExplanation: Lisinopril therapy is an ACE inhibitor antihypertension medication, which would be the most likely intervention to reduce this patient's risk for recurrent hypertension-associated intraparenchymal hemorrhagic stroke. The patient presents with progressively worsening headache and a focal neurologic deficit, characteristic for an intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Emergent noncontrast CT of the head is indicated for evaluation, which in this patient demonstrates a region of hyperdensity in the right putamen, consistent with an intraparenchymal hemorrhage. The greatest risk factor for an intraparenchymal hemorrhage is poorly or uncontrolled hypertension. Hypertension most commonly results in hemorrhages within the basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus, and/or pons. Initiation of antihypertensive therapy to reduce the patient's blood pressure would decrease his risk for recurrent hemorrhagic stroke.
incorrectExplanation: Alcohol cessation (Choice A), smoking cessation (Choice B), and weight loss (Choice C), while critical to improve the overall health of the patient, less directly result in reduced risk for recurrent hemorrhagic stroke as compared to direct management of hypertension. Improved body habitus and dietary changes may contribute to improved overall health and blood pressure, although lisinopril therapy would have a greater and faster impact on reducing the patient's blood pressure. Atorvastatin therapy (Choice D) would assist in decreasing the patient's cholesterol, although this would primarily decrease risk for an ischemic stroke, not recurrent hemorrhagic stroke. Clopidogrel therapy (Choice E) would be contraindicated in a patient with a history of hemorrhagic stroke as clopidogrel is an antiplatelet medication that would increase the patient's risk for hemorrhage.

questionStem: A 32-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of irregular menses for 3 years. Menses occur at 35- to 60-day intervals. Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She has no history of serious illness but has been overweight most of her adult life. She is sexually active with her husband of 3 years and uses condoms consistently. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 77 kg (170 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m2. Her blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows moderate coarse hair over the upper lip, chin, and abdomen. Abdominal and pelvic examinations show no abnormalities. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 4 μU/mL, β-hCG concentration of less than 2 mIU/mL, and prolactin concentration of 18 ng/mL. Pelvic ultrasonography shows no abnormalities. In addition to recommending weight loss, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Oral contraceptive therapy is the first-line therapy for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) in patients who are not attempting to conceive. The patient presents with irregular menses, hirsutism, and increased body weight, without abnormal thyroid or prolactin lab values. This is characteristic for PCOS. PCOS demonstrates excess androgens and can present with polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, oligo/anovulation, or clinical/biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, of which two are required for the diagnosis. The patient demonstrates a normal pelvic ultrasound, although delineation of polycystic ovaries is not required since she exhibits signs of oligo/anovulation and hyperandrogenism. PCOS increases the risk for metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus. For patients who are not attempting to conceive, first-line therapy consists of weight loss and treatment with a combination of oral contraceptives and/or metformin. If the patient is attempting to conceive, therapy should include weight loss, clomiphene (to improve successful ovulation), and/or metformin.
incorrectExplanation: Oral medroxyprogesterone therapy (Choice B) is a type of contraceptive consisting of only progestin. Progestin administration would not improve the patient's anovulation, which requires the combination effects of estrogen and progestin in oral contraceptives. Additionally, adverse effects of medroxyprogesterone include weight gain and irregular periods, which would not improve the patient's PCOS symptoms. Oral prednisone therapy (Choice C) and oral thyroid therapy (Choice D) are not indicated in the treatment of PCOS. Oral prednisone is indicated in a variety of inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, although in this patient the adverse effects of weight gain and metabolic syndrome would be deleterious. Oral thyroid therapy is not indicated given the patient's normal TSH concentration, indicating she is euthyroid. Depot leuprolide injection (Choice E) is a GnRH analog, which serves to downregulate GnRH receptors in the pituitary and results in decreased production of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. Leuprolide is utilized for the treatment of a variety of conditions, including precocious puberty, infertility, and endometriosis.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a 3-minute episode of unconsciousness. The patient says that the episode began with an impending sense of feeling ill while watching television. He quickly became confused, swayed in his chair, and fell to the floor. He had no bowel or bladder incontinence during this episode. His mental status spontaneously recovered fully within 3 minutes. He has a 10-year history of hypertension well controlled with hydrochlorothiazide. He had a myocardial infarction 4 years ago. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m². His pulse is 86/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 124/86 mm Hg. Neurologic and cardiac examinations show normal findings. An ECG shows Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia (VT) refers to the sudden onset of VT, defined as three or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions. This results in a wide QRS complex tachyarrhythmia. Risk factors include underlying structural heart disease, history of coronary artery disease, or myocardial infarction. Nonsustained VT lasts for less than 30 seconds, while sustained VT persists longer than 30 seconds and presents with varying symptoms such as palpitations and syncope. While an episode of VT may be transient, if sustained, it may require treatment with anti-arrhythmic medications or cardioversion. Class one or three antiarrhythmics are the frequent first-line therapy for stable, sustained VT. Synchronized cardioversion may be necessary in cases of unstable, sustained VT, and defibrillation is required for pulseless VT. Syncope in the setting of VT typically persists for the duration of the episode.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Hypoglycemia (Choice A) is a common cause of syncope, most often in patients with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus or an underlying insulinoma. Syncope secondary to hypoglycemia requires treatment with dextrose and/or glucagon and would not be expected to spontaneously resolve without treatment. Additionally, the patient does not exhibit risk factors for hypoglycemia, and given his cardiac risk factors, arrhythmogenic syncope is more likely.

Pulmonary embolus (PE) (Choice C) can result in syncope in the setting of a massive PE, which would present with tachycardia and hypotension, with possible right heart strain signs on ECG (eg, “S1Q3T3” pattern).

Seizure (Choice D), such as a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, would present with sudden onset syncope with characteristic movement dependent on the type of generalized seizure. Typically, the patient would present in a postictal state with delayed recovery of mental status.

Transient ischemic attack (Choice E) is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without infarction. Transient ischemic attack resulting in syncope does not typically present with a postictal state.

questionStem: A 62-year-old man has a 2-day history of generalized weakness and inability to walk without assistance 7 days after admission to the intensive care unit for treatment of fever, cough, and a left upper lobe consolidation. Treatment with ceftriaxone and azithromycin initially improved his symptoms. He has not had fever for the past 2 days. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus. His current medications are ceftriaxone, heparin, omeprazole, and insulin glargine. A peripheral catheter is in place; there is no central access. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the skin shows no lesions. On pulmonary examination, rhonchi are heard in the left upper lobe. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin Day 5: 10.8 g/dL, Day 7: 10 g/dL; Leukocyte count Day 5: 11,500/mm3, Day 7: 12,000/mm3; Platelet count Day 5: 330,000/mm3, Day 7: 90,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Add epoetin alfa to the medication regimen
choices.B: Discontinue ceftriaxone and begin physical therapy
choices.C: Switch from ceftriaxone to piperacillin and tazobactam therapy
choices.D: Switch from heparin to direct thrombin inhibitor therapy
choices.E: Switch from heparin to low-molecular-weight heparin therapy

correctExplanation: Switch from heparin to direct thrombin inhibitor therapy is indicated for the treatment of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). HIT typically occurs between 5 and 10 days after the initiation of heparin therapy. It results from the development of IgG antibodies against the complex of heparin and platelet factor 4. This complex leads to the activation of platelets, which can cause thrombosis, typically venous, and consumption of platelets. This abnormal activation yields progressively decreasing platelet counts, which typically hit their lowest point at greater than 50% from their initial level. Treatment requires cessation of all heparin-related products (eg, unfractionated heparin and low-molecular-weight heparin). The patient should be transitioned to a direct thrombin inhibitor or direct factor Xa inhibitor to ensure adequate anticoagulation without worsening the thrombocytopenia.
incorrectExplanation: Add epoetin alfa to the medication regimen (Choice A) would result in increased red blood cell production from the bone marrow, not platelet production. Epoetin alfa is an analog of erythropoietin (EPO). This is commonly utilized in the setting of chronic end-stage kidney disease for the treatment of normocytic anemia from impaired EPO production. Discontinue ceftriaxone and begin physical therapy (Choice B) is not the best option as ceftriaxone is necessary to treat her pneumonia, and it is less likely to cause thrombocytopenia than heparin over this abrupt time course. Switch from ceftriaxone to piperacillin and tazobactam therapy (Choice C) would only be indicated if the patient developed a hospital or ventilator-associated pneumonia, for which broad-spectrum antibiotics are necessary. Rather, this patient presents with community acquired pneumonia (CAP). Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are first-line therapies for CAP. Switch from heparin to low-molecular-weight heparin therapy (Choice E) would cause further worsening of the patient’s HIT, as low-molecular-weight heparin is a subtype of heparin and would further propagate the antibody complex formation and activation of platelets. Instead, the patient requires transition to a direct thrombin inhibitor or factor Xa inhibitor for anticoagulation.

questionStem: An asymptomatic 24-year-old man who is HIV positive comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He has been seen by a physician regularly since he was diagnosed 3 years ago and has been following all recommendations. He currently takes no medications. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 42%, Leukocyte count 4000/mm³, CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 550/mm³ (Normal ≥ 500), Plasma HIV viral load 2000 copies/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?

choices.C: Two-drug antiretroviral therapy and Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carinii) prophylaxis
choices.E: Three-drug antiretroviral therapy and P. jiroveci prophylaxis

correctExplanation: All HIV positive patients should be on 3 drug ART as soon as possible (regardless of CD4+ counts).
incorrectExplanation: Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis is recommended once the CD4+ <200 (this patient doesn’t need it since his CD4+ is 550).

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up examination. Six weeks ago, she was diagnosed with sinusitis and began a 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate therapy. She has occasional nonproductive cough; she otherwise feels well. During the past 6 years, she has had eight episodes of sinusitis treated with amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and azithromycin. One episode required a 1-month course of amoxicillin therapy. The patient also has had two episodes of bacterial pneumonia during the past 3 years that resolved with moxifloxacin therapy. She currently takes no medications. Her maternal uncle died of pneumonia at the age of 28 years. The patient is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 64 kg (140 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Scattered rhonchi are heard over the right lower lung base. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Results of a complete blood count, liver and kidney function testing, and HIV antibody serologic testing are within the reference ranges. A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses shows mucosal thickening of the maxillary, sphenoid, and ethmoid sinuses. A CT scan of the chest shows bronchial thickening and dilation of the bronchi in the lower lobe of the right lung. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Recurrent infections, as seen in this patient, raise concern for an underlying primary immunodeficiency. Primary immunodeficiencies may result from abnormalities of acquired immunity (B-cell, T-cell), innate immunity, or combined dysfunction. Specifically, a decreased, absent, or aberrant production of immunoglobulin by B-cells can result in recurrent sinopulmonary infections, leading to multiple recurrent sinus infections and pneumonia, which this patient demonstrates. These recurrent pulmonary infections can lead to the development of bronchiectasis over time. For further differentiation of the patient's primary immunodeficiency, quantitative immunoglobulin testing should be performed to delineate the patient's immunologic pathophysiology. B-cell disorders include such diseases as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, selective IgA deficiency, and common variable immunodeficiency. Given the patient's age and presentation, common variable immunodeficiency is the most likely etiology since it typically presents in early adulthood and characteristically leads to increased sinopulmonary infections.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and E. Bone marrow biopsies (Choice A) are an invasive form of diagnostic evaluation, necessary if a primary bone marrow pathology is expected such as lymphoproliferative disorders or otherwise unexplained cytopenias. Bronchoalveolar lavage (Choice B) is recommended to definitively identify the infectious organism present in the setting of severe and/or persistent pneumonia. Open lung biopsy (Choice C) may be indicated for a variety of clinical scenarios (eg, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary nodule/mass), but is not necessary for the diagnosis of an immunodeficiency. Sputum culture for acid-fast bacilli (Choice E) most commonly is used to evaluate for a mycobacterial infection.

questionStem: An unconscious 37-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found in an abandoned house. On arrival, her temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. She is unresponsive to painful stimuli. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Her serum creatinine concentration is 3 mg/dL, and blood alcohol concentration is 200 mg/dL. The remainder of the toxicology screening is negative. Urinalysis shows pigmented casts. Serum studies are most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: Rhabdomyolysis is the result of infectious, ischemic, or traumatic skeletal muscle cell lysis, with release of intracellular contents into the extracellular, vascular, and lymphatic spaces. The patient was found down, likely in a state of prolonged immobilization following intoxication, which can result in traumatic necrosis of large muscle groups, often the gluteus maximus and erector spinae groups in patients who were supine. Myoglobin is released into the blood, which is nephrotoxic and can lead to pigmented casts in the urine. This can result in acute kidney injury from tubular necrosis. Creatine kinase is an enzyme found primarily in muscle, which is released in states of myocyte destruction or turnover and serves as an accurate surrogate marker for myocyte injury as is seen in this patient with rhabdomyolysis.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and D. Decreased phosphorus concentration (Choice A) would not be expected in the setting of rhabdomyolysis, as it is an intracellular ion that is often released into serum in such cases. Sodium (Choice B) is generally regulated by the pituitary gland and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, neither of which are immediately affected in rhabdomyolysis. Acidosis can occur in the setting of prolonged immobilization, rhabdomyolysis, and lactic acidosis, for which the bicarbonate level would be expected to fall because of its active role in buffering the serum pH (Choice C). Calcium levels often fall in the setting of rhabdomyolysis due to dystrophic calcium deposition (Choice D).

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because she is concerned about her risk for osteoporosis. She has hypertension and deep venous thrombosis. Current medications include metoprolol and warfarin. There is no personal or family history of fractures. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her blood pressure is 132/82 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. A DEXA scan shows findings consistent with osteoporosis. In addition to calcium and vitamin D supplementation, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Correct Answer: A. Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease characterized by diffusely low bone density. Evaluation for osteoporosis occurs through performance of a DEXA scan and is defined as a bone mineral density less than 2.5 standard deviations compared to a young, normal population (T-score). The most common risk factors for the development of osteoporosis are age, smoking, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, and estrogen-depleting conditions in women. Osteoporosis is often asymptomatic but increases the risk for fractures, most commonly involving the hip, vertebrae, and distal radius. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation are the first line for treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. Reduction of active osteoporotic risk factors should also be pursued. Weight-bearing exercises are recommended to slow deterioration of bone mineral density. Bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate) inhibit osteoclast activity. They are utilized once an individual is diagnosed with osteoporosis to reduce further loss of bone mineral density.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Calcitonin (Choice B) is a native hormone which inhibits osteoclast activity and reabsorption of calcium within the renal tubules. It is rarely used for the treatment of osteoporosis given its cost and side effect profile, but can be used in the setting of severe, symptomatic hypercalcemia. Estrogen (Choice C) does result in positive bony remodeling, which would in theory lead to increased bone mineral density, although administration of estrogen results in a significantly increased risk for the development of life-threatening venous thrombosis. Isoflavones (Choice D) are postulated to improve postmenopausal symptoms and delay osteoporosis, although there is currently insufficient data on their effectiveness and safety. Raloxifene (Choice E) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator, which acts as an agonist for positive bony remodeling from increased osteoblast activity. It is useful in the prevention of osteoporosis, but due to off-target effects is generally third line following bisphosphonates.

questionStem: A 57-year-old homeless man is admitted to the hospital because of a 5-day history of moderate neck pain and fever. He has HIV infection and hepatitis C. He takes no medications. He uses intravenous heroin three times weekly. He does not smoke cigarettes and drinks alcohol occasionally. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. There is no photophobia. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm; a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. The neck is tender over the lower cervical spine with no warmth or erythema. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 400/mm3 (Normal≥500), and HIV viral load is 75,000 copies/mL. A chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the cervical spine shows destructive changes in C5 and C6 and collapse of the intervening disc space. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's neck pain?

choices.A: Contiguous spread of organism from adjacent soft-tissue process
choices.B: Direct inoculation of the soft tissues of the neck

correctExplanation: Correct Answer: D. Discitis-osteomyelitis refers to an acute infection of a vertebral disc and the adjacent vertebral bodies, most commonly secondary to S. aureus. In adults, it most commonly occurs from direct spread from an adjacent soft tissue infection and less likely from hematogenous seeding of bacteria to that site. In children and intravenous drug users, hematogenous seeding is more common given the propensity for bacteremia and distant seeding of the bacteria to the involved site. In intravenous drug users, S. aureus and Pseudomonas are the two most common pathogens. On imaging, discitis-osteomyelitis can present with destructive changes of the vertebral bone with collapse of the disc space. Given the patient has a systolic murmur and fever in the setting of intravenous drug use, there is the potential he may have infective endocarditis, which would serve as a source of hematogenous bacterial seeding to the vertebral column.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Contiguous spread of an organism from an adjacent soft tissue infection (Choice A) is the most common modality for the development of osteomyelitis in adults, although this patient did not have a prior soft tissue infection. Direct inoculation (Choice B) occurs in the setting of penetrating trauma or surgery, neither of which this patient demonstrates. Granulomatous inflammation (Choice C) may occur in the setting of various inflammatory and infectious processes, with vertebral tuberculosis (Pott's disease) a possible explanation for discitis-osteomyelitis, although this patient is an intravenous drug user with possible infective endocarditis, making hematogenous seeding more probable. Reactivation of a latent organism (Choice E) may refer to any number of various infectious processes (eg, reactivation tuberculosis, herpes simplex viruses), although this patient's discitis-osteomyelitis is related to intravenous drug use and possible infective endocarditis with subsequent hematogenous seeding.

questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He has no history of serious illness. Both of his parents died of cerebral infarction in their 70s. He smokes one-half pack of cigarettes daily and drinks one 6-oz glass of wine daily. He takes no medications. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 91 kg (200 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 170/95 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. On cardiac examination, an S4 is heard at the cardiac apex. There are no murmurs. No bruits are heard over the neck. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies obtained after fasting show a glucose concentration of 140 mg/dL and cholesterol concentration of 250 mg/dL. Which of the following measures is most likely to decrease this patient's risk for cerebral infarction?

choices.B: Decreasing alcohol intake to 12 ounces weekly

correctExplanation: There are a number of modifiable risk factors that lead to an increased risk for cerebral infarction. Among these, hypertension remains the largest risk factor because of its consequent ability to result in vascular remodeling and progression of atherosclerotic disease. While ideal blood pressure targets remain controversial, a blood pressure of >140/90 has been shown to significantly increase a patient's risk of stroke. Additionally, the patient in the vignette demonstrates consequences of chronic hypertension including an S4 heart sound, possibly indicating left ventricular hypertrophy and a resultant stiff ventricular wall. Given the patient's elevated blood pressure and its known relationship with significantly increased risk of stroke, the patient would most benefit from appropriate antihypertensive therapy to decrease his future risk of cerebral infarction.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and E. Cigarette smoking, binge alcohol consumption, high dietary fat intake, and diabetes mellitus are all associated with increased risk of atherosclerosis and the development of cerebral infarction. While smoking cessation (Choice A), decreased alcohol intake (Choice B), low-fat diet (Choice C), and hypoglycemic therapy (Choice E) may decrease the risk of cerebral infarction in this patient, they are less significant on this patient's risk for stroke when compared with appropriate antihypertensive management.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of a painful rash on his right index finger, low-grade fever, and swollen lymph nodes in his right armpit. There is no family history of serious illness. He drinks one alcoholic beverage daily. He does not smoke. He works as a dentist. His temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. A photograph of the right index finger is shown. There is right axillary lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Herpetic whitlow represents an acute viral infection of the finger by herpes simplex virus (HSV 1 or 2). It typically results in pain and erythema with non-purulent vesicle formation. This is classically seen in dentists due to oral-cutaneous inoculation. There can be reactive lymphadenopathy of the adjacent upper extremity and axilla. This acute infection is best treated with acyclovir, a guanosine analog which preferentially inhibits DNA polymerase for HSV and varicella zoster virus.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, D, E, and F. Topical erythromycin (Choice A) is an antibiotic ointment typically used for the treatment of acne vulgaris. Topical hydrocortisone therapy (Choice B) can be utilized for a variety of inflammatory skin conditions (eg, eczema) but would not be effective in the setting of an acute HSV skin infection. Oral dicloxacillin (Choice D) is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin used clinically to treat methicillin-sensitive S. aureus infections. Oral prednisolone therapy (Choice E) is a glucocorticoid regimen used in a variety of systemic inflammatory conditions (eg, severe persistent asthma) but would be ineffective against an acute HSV skin infection. Incision and drainage (Choice F) is utilized for treatment of organized abscesses to release pus and debris from the abscess. The patient demonstrates vesicles along the index finger secondary to HSV infection but does not have a clinical manifestation of an abscess of the finger such as fluctuant induration.

questionStem: A 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because she says that she is having "the worst headache of my life." It began abruptly while she was eating dinner 2 hours ago. She has a history of hypertension treated with diuretics. She is lying quietly with her eyes closed. She has difficulty talking and concentrating because of the pain, but is fully oriented. Her blood pressure is 180/98 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate neck rigidity. Cranial nerves, reflexes, and sensory examination are normal. Examination of cerebrospinal fluid shows an opening pressure of 170 mm H2O, erythrocyte count of 86,000/mm3, and leukocyte count of 5/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage most often presents from a ruptured intracranial aneurysm in the setting of hypertension. These are often “berry” aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, and typically occur with a “thunderclap” worst-headache-of-life, neck stiffness, and photophobia. The aneurysm rupture may have been precipitated by an event increasing her mean arterial pressure, which would increase stress on the aneurysmal vascular wall. Lumbar puncture demonstrates a significant number of red blood cells, which are typical in the setting of subarachnoid hemorrhage. A CT scan of the head without contrast is typically obtained in the acute setting to confirm the presence of subarachnoid blood, and if confirmed, further angiographic imaging of the head is necessary to identify the presence of an aneurysm.
incorrectExplanation: Hypertensive urgency or emergency (Choice A) can present with a headache, but hemorrhagic cerebrospinal fluid makes a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm a more likely diagnosis. Epidural hematoma and subdural hematoma (Choices B and G) typically occur in the setting of trauma. They often cause headache and can present with signs of acute elevations in intracranial pressure due to an expanding lesion compressing the brain. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice C) presents most commonly in younger, overweight females taking vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazol. It is usually associated with a holocephalic headache and blurry vision. Meningitis (Choice D) classically presents with an acute headache, fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness, with variable etiologies from bacterial, viral, or fungal sources. Leukocytes would be elevated on cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Migraine headaches (Choice E) characteristically recur over time and may present with a pulsatile, unilateral, or bilateral headache with associated photophobia or phonophobia. They are often triggered by foods, medications, noises, menses, or illness.

questionStem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of progressive swelling of her left calf. Ten years ago, she had a thrombus in her left leg and was treated with anticoagulants for 4 months. She currently takes no medications. Her pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination shows mild edema and prominent varicose veins of the distal left lower extremity. There is an 8-cm area of hyperpigmentation over the left ankle. Examination of the right lower extremity shows no abnormalities. Peripheral pulses are normal. Ultrasonography of the lower extremities shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's edema?
correctExplanation: Valvular insufficiency is a common complication of deep venous thrombosis. As a thrombus occludes the cross-sectional area of a deep vein, the valves, which originate from the walls of the veins, become involved in the thrombus either through compression against the wall of the vessel or through incorporation into the thrombus during propagation. When the thrombus resolves, the residual valve may be dysfunctional from damage to the leaflets, annulus, or diameter of the native vessel. This prevents the valve from functioning effectively and results in retrograde venous flow secondary to gravity. Inadequate venous drainage of the lower extremities can result in varicose veins, chronic edema, and stasis dermatitis.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and D. Cellulitis (Choice A) is characterized by inflammation in the skin and demonstrates erythema, induration, warmth, and edema. Most commonly, it is acute and results from a bacterial infection of the skin. Obstruction of the iliac vein (Choice B) would present with edema of the entire left lower extremity as opposed to the calf in isolation. Further, the patient's ultrasound was normal, without evidence of an obstruction. On duplex ultrasound, the iliac vessels would not necessarily be visualized, although doppler venous waveforms can suggest a proximal obstruction if present. Obstruction of lymph channels (Choice C) results in nonpitting edema of the affected extremity, though would be less likely given the patient's anatomically correlated history of a deep venous thrombosis and lack of infectious (eg, filariasis), surgical, malignant, or traumatic history to explain injury to the lymphatic system. Saphenous vein reflux (Choice D) could explain lower extremity edema and varicose vein development; however, it is a superficial vein and this patient has no known history of thrombosis or structural damage to it.

questionStem: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of severe left ear pain. At the onset of pain, he flushed his ear with water; the pain has become increasingly severe since then. He has no history of ear problems. He has a 30-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus poorly controlled with insulin. Examination shows moist debris and edema of the left ear canal. Granulation tissue is seen on the floor of the ear canal. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 18,000/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 78%, Lymphocytes 22%, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 100 mm/h, Serum glucose 450 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Correct Answer: F. Necrotizing otitis externa refers to infection of the external ear canal typically from Pseudomonas or Enterobacteriaceae, which both thrive in moist environments. It is frequently seen in patients with poorly controlled diabetes and immunocompromised states. Classically, it presents with external ear pain exacerbated with movement of the tragus or pinna, purulent discharge, and an edematous/erythematous external ear canal often containing granulation tissue. When the infection is severe and has infiltrated outside the external ear canal causing extensive tissue destruction, it is termed necrotizing (or malignant) otitis externa, which requires treatment with intravenous antibiotics. Otitis externa is not always necrotizing. The non-necrotizing variant is commonly known as “swimmer’s ear,” and presents with mild external ear pain, watery discharge, swelling, and erythema of the external acoustic meatus. Treatment of non-necrotizing otitis externa consists of adequately cleaning the ear, acidifying the canal, and administering fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin) ear drops.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E. Acute mastoiditis (Choice A) presents with erythema and tenderness posterior to the ear, over the mastoid bone. It often results as a complication from otitis media. Acute otitis media (Choice B) classically occurs in children, often from viral or bacterial pathogens. It presents with ear pain, often with fever, and with an erythematous tympanic membrane with retractiontype pus or middle ear effusion. Angiocentric T-cell lymphoma (Choice C) is a rare cutaneous malignancy often involving natural killer cells, and typically presents as single or multiple plaques/nodules, which can sometimes ulcerate. Chronic otitis media with effusion (Choice D) presents with chronic middle ear pain and a retractiontype effusion, a feature not seen on this patient’s exam. Fungal otitis externa (Choice E) would present similarly to this patient’s exam but would be less likely than a bacterial cause; it may be more likely subacute and indolent.

questionStem: A previously healthy 57-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for evaluation of a 3-week history of increasing fatigue, constipation, urinary frequency, and increased thirst. She appears lethargic. Her pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 150/70 mm Hg. Examination shows dry mucous membranes. Serum studies show a calcium concentration of 15.2 mg/dL, phosphorus concentration of 2.1 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone concentration of 800 pg/mL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's polyuria and volume depletion?
correctExplanation: Correct Answer: F. Primary hyperparathyroidism results in hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia secondary to the aberrant increased production of parathyroid hormone (PTH). The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a parathyroid adenoma, with parathyroid hyperplasia and carcinoma additional possibilities. Common symptoms of primary hyperparathyroidism are secondary to the patient's resultant hypercalcemia and include recurrent nephrolithiasis, bone pain from osseous resorption, polyuria, dehydration, constipation, and psychiatric disturbances. Polyuria and associated volume depletion are secondary to the direct effects of hypercalcemia on the kidney, which results in renal resistance and lack of response to anti-diuretic hormone (ADH), known as nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The resistance to ADH results in insufficient aquaporin expression in the collecting tubules of renal nephrons, leading to increased urine volume, which manifests clinically as polyuria and volume depletion.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E. Allergic interstitial nephritis (Choice A) results in pyuria (predominantly eosinophils) and azotemia often related to the use of certain classes of medications such as diuretics, penicillins, proton pump inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and sulfonamides. Central diabetes insipidus (Choice B) results in polyuria and volume depletion secondary to insufficient production of ADH from a brain injury or lesion. Chronic pyelonephritis (Choice C) often occurs in patients prone to recurrent episodes of acute pyelonephritis, with risk factors such as chronic obstructing renal stones or vesicoureteral reflux. Glycosuria (Choice D) refers to glucose in the urine, often in patients with hyperglycemia secondary to diabetes mellitus. Hypertensive nephropathy (Choice E) is a common cause of chronic renal failure, resulting from glomerular damage from chronic hypertension.

questionStem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-day history of fever and severe abdominal pain. His only medication is glyburide. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). Abdominal examination shows moderate left lower quadrant tenderness with guarding but no rebound. His serum creatinine concentration is 1.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. This patient should receive which of the following prior to a CT scan of the abdomen with intravenous contrast?
correctExplanation: Correct Answer: E. Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) results from the toxic effect of intravenous contrast on the tubular cells of the kidney and may result in impaired renal function. This patient presents with a fever and abdominal pain and will require a contrast-enhanced CT scan to further assess the etiology. His creatinine is elevated, which may place him at a higher risk for the development of CIN. To prevent or decrease the patient's risk of CIN, he should receive an intravenous 0.9% saline infusion. Intravenous isotonic fluid administration assists in promoting renal excretion and reducing nephrotoxic effects of iodinated contrast.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Atrial natriuretic peptide (Choice A) may promote diuresis though has not been shown to prevent CIN. Dopamine (Choice B) is considered a nephroprotective inotrope. At low concentrations, it can theoretically increase renal blood flow. It does not have a role in preventing CIN. Furosemide (Choice C) is a loop diuretic, which would result in increased urine production. Loop diuretics had been shown to reduce the risk of CIN when used in conjunction with matched intravenous fluid hydration. Loop diuretics should not be used as a sole preventative measure for CIN as the diuretic may result in hemodynamically significant hypovolemia which could worsen any contrast-associated acute kidney injury. Mannitol (Choice D) is an osmotic diuretic most commonly used to lower intracranial and intraocular pressure in acute elevations. Forced diuresis with mannitol is not currently recommended for the prevention of CIN.

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has chronic renal failure secondary to glomerulonephritis. She has received hemodialysis three times weekly for 2 years. She is on a waiting list for a renal transplant. Examination shows no abnormalities. Her serum calcium concentration is 8.2 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's hypocalcemia?

choices.A: Decreased absorption due to decreased serum 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol concentration
choices.B: Decreased absorption due to decreased serum magnesium concentration
choices.C: Decreased absorption due to increased serum ionized calcium concentration
choices.D: Increased calcium binding by phosphate in the small bowel
choices.E: Increased suppression of parathyroid hormone due to increased serum ionized phosphorus concentration

correctExplanation: Active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) is synthesized through cutaneous, hepatic, and renal routes, with the final conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol in the kidney via 1-alpha hydroxylase. Patients with chronic kidney disease have diminished capacity for native vitamin D synthesis because of underlying renal parenchymal damage. The decreased production of active vitamin D results in impaired gastrointestinal uptake of dietary calcium, leading to hypocalcemia. This, in turn, leads to elevations in parathyroid hormone and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
incorrectExplanation: Magnesium (Choice B) is commonly coabsorbed in the small intestine, notably facilitating absorption of potassium. It does not have a prominent role in the absorption of calcium in patients with renal failure. Patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal failure are most commonly hypocalcemic, including both bound and free ionized calcium (Choice C). Patients with renal failure typically develop an elevated serum phosphate because of impaired renal excretion of phosphate from tubular dysfunction (Choice D), which does not necessarily relate to increased intraluminal phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract. Serum parathyroid hormone in renal failure is characteristically elevated by hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia (Choice E).

questionStem: A 47-year-old man with alcoholism is transferred from the hospital to a drug rehabilitation facility. On arrival, examination shows hyperreflexia and a tremor in both hands when they are outstretched. His serum calcium concentration is 8.1 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely additional serum electrolyte abnormality in this patient?
correctExplanation: C. Patients with alcohol use disorder often develop multiple vitamin, mineral, and electrolyte deficiencies due to malnutrition from lower dietary intake and the concomitant diuretic effect of alcohol, leading to excessive urinary losses. This patient's examination demonstrates neurologic symptoms, including hyperreflexia and tremor in the setting of alcoholism. Magnesium deficiency is common in patients with alcoholism and often presents with hyperreflexia and tremor. Additional symptoms of magnesium deficiency can include seizures, muscle spasms, and dysrhythmias (eg, Torsades de Pointes).
incorrectExplanation: A, B, D, and E. Hypochloremia (Choice A) infrequently occurs in isolation, and when present, is usually associated with imbalances in sodium, acid-base, or volume status. Most patients do not have symptoms of hypochloremia independent of the presenting condition, such as dehydration from diarrhea, vomiting, or central nervous system symptoms associated with concomitant hyponatremia. Hypokalemia (Choice B), while often occurring in alcoholism, presents commonly with cardiac conduction abnormalities, such as acquired long-QT syndrome or dysrhythmias, but does not typically present with peripheral neurologic deficits. Hyponatremia (Choice D) is often asymptomatic if chronic and slowly developing, although when acute, it is associated with central nervous system symptoms such as headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, delirium, weakness, seizures, and coma. Hypophosphatemia (Choice E) can occur in the setting of nutritional deficiency, especially anorexia nervosa or bulimia. Symptoms result from depletion of adenosine triphosphate and include muscle weakness, cardiorespiratory depression, and neurologic depression such as seizure or coma.

questionStem: A previously healthy 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of frequent pain with urination and episodes of loss of urine. She has no history of similar symptoms, and she has not had pelvic pain or change in bowel function. Menses occur at regular intervals and last 4 days; her last menstrual period was 10 days ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. The external genitalia, vagina, and cervix appear normal. There is no cervical motion or uterine tenderness, but the bladder is tender to palpation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) affect women more frequently than men and may present with lower and/or upper urinary tract symptoms. Lower urinary tract symptoms include increased urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and dysuria. Upper urinary tract symptoms include flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, and systemic signs/symptoms such as fevers and rigors. Diagnosis of a lower urinary tract infection should be made based on clinical symptoms and supported by increased leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis along with growth of culprit organisms on urine culture. Uncomplicated UTIs should be treated with nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, cephalexin, or a fluoroquinolone depending on local sensitivity and resistance patterns. Criteria for a complicated UTI, which would require longer courses of antibiotics, include male gender, urinary obstruction, renal transplant, recent urinary tract instrumentation, or the presence of a urinary catheter.
incorrectExplanation: Oxybutynin (Choice B) is an anti-muscarinic medication used to treat urge incontinence from an overactive bladder and detrusor instability. Intermittent self-catheterization (Choice C) is utilized for the treatment of overflow incontinence from incomplete emptying secondary to detrusor underactivity or bladder outlet obstruction. Catheterization increases the risk of urinary tract infection, although intermittent self-catheterization imparts less risk than an indwelling Foley or suprapubic catheter. Sacral nerve stimulation (Choice D) is used for the treatment of bladder and bowel incontinence. The S2-S4 nerve roots are modulated to allow for improved voiding, as these play a crucial role in the autonomic regulation of micturition. The midurethral sling procedure (Choice E) is used to treat stress incontinence and entails a surgical procedure utilizing synthetic mesh to support the urethra.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of fatigue. She first noted her fatigue after the birth of her second child; pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. During both pregnancies, she was told she had anemia. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume 66 μm³ Reticulocyte count 0.3% Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows: Hemoglobin A₂ 5% (N=2%-4%) Hemoglobin F 2% (N=0%-2%) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Anemia can be subdivided on the basis of mean corpuscular volume (MCV) into microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic categories, and then on the basis of the etiology for red blood cell loss (eg, underproduction, sequestration, extracorporeal loss, or early destruction or lysis of cells). This patient demonstrates a microcytic anemia (MCV < 80 μm³), common etiologies of which include iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, and sideroblastic anemia. Her fraction of hemoglobin A₂ is abnormally elevated, suggestive of an impairment in heme synthesis and diagnostic of beta-thalassemia trait.
incorrectExplanation: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Choice A) and sickle cell disease (Choice D) most often present with a normocytic anemia and would not be expected to present with an abnormal fraction of hemoglobin A₂. Iron deficiency anemia (Choice B), lead poisoning (Choice C), and sideroblastic anemia (Choice E) result in impaired synthesis of heme and/or hemoglobin, and present with a normocytic (early) or microcytic (later) anemia. However, hemoglobin electrophoresis would be normal in these cases.

questionStem: A 27-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of irregular menses. During this time, she has had vaginal spotting so frequently that she does not know the dates of her actual menstrual periods. Previously, menses occurred at regular 28-day intervals. She also reports increased hair growth over the face, chest, and lower abdomen. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows coarse hair over the upper lip, chin, and abdomen. Abdominal and pelvic examinations show no abnormalities. Her serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentration is 75 μg/mL (N=0.5–5.4). An overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows no suppression of cortisol. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Measurement of fasting serum cortisol concentration

correctExplanation: D. Cushing syndrome is characterized by excess production of cortisol. This results in symptoms such as oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, weight gain, skin changes, osteoporosis, and hyperglycemia. Non-suppression of cortisol on overnight dexamethasone suppression test is diagnostic of Cushing syndrome. There are multiple potential etiologies of Cushing syndrome, including pituitary adenoma, adrenal tumor, or ectopic paraneoplastic ACTH secretion (eg, small-cell lung cancer). Along with the increased production of cortisol, Cushing syndrome from an adrenal etiology can also result in increased concentrations of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) produced within the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex. Elevated DHEA-S can also occur in the setting of adrenocortical carcinoma and adrenal hyperplasia. Given the increased DHEA-S, the likely etiology is localized to the adrenal gland. To further assess the patient's pathologic production of cortisol, a CT scan of the abdomen would be the next best step in management to investigate the presence of a functional adrenal nodule or hyperplasia.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and E. The first step in the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome involves one of three tests: 24-hour urine free cortisol, late night salivary cortisol, or inadequate suppression on 1 mg (low-dose) overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Fasting serum cortisol concentration (Choice A) would be inaccurate for the evaluation and diagnosis of Cushing syndrome. Serum potassium concentration (Choice B) is variable in the setting of Cushing syndrome and may be within normal limits or mildly decreased. This is secondary to cortisol's mild affinity for mineralocorticoid receptors (eg, aldosterone) in the kidney, resulting in increased excretion of potassium in the urine. The patient's irregular menses are explained by excessive cortisol and DHEA-S from Cushing syndrome, which does not require ultrasound of the pelvis for further investigation (Choice C), as the etiology is likely secondary to an adrenal process in this instance. MRI of the brain (Choice E) is useful for evaluation of intracranial pathology, including pituitary adenomas. Given the patient's elevated DHEA-S, the etiology for the patient's elevated cortisol is likely within the adrenal gland, not the pituitary gland.

questionStem: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of increasing fatigue, weakness, malaise, and darkening of his skin. During this period, he has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. He now has difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. He appears cachectic. His blood pressure is 160/98 mm Hg while sitting. Examination shows hyperpigmentation of the skin and proximal muscle wasting and mild pitting edema at the ankles. His hemoglobin concentration is 11.5 g/dL, serum potassium concentration is 3.0 mEq/L, and serum glucose concentration is 130 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Small cell carcinoma of the lung

correctExplanation: The combination of the patient's history of smoking, weight loss, fatigue, weakness, and cachexia is suggestive of an underlying malignancy. Small-cell carcinoma of the lung is associated with multiple paraneoplastic endocrine, neurologic, dermatologic, and musculoskeletal syndromes. This patient has developed paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome, marked by proximal muscle wasting, hyperpigmentation, hypertension, edema, elevated blood glucose, and hypokalemia due to an elevation in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) leading to chronic adrenal hyperstimulation and unregulated, overproduction of cortisol. In small-cell lung cancer, the ACTH is typically released ectopically from the malignancy itself.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and D. Adrenal insufficiency (Choice A) presents with hypotension, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, weakness, and variable metabolic and acid-base derangements, depending on the level (primary vs. secondary) of the lesion. Bronchial carcinoid (Choice B) is a less likely cause of pulmonary malignancy as compared with small-cell carcinoma and presents with syndromes related to neurotransmitter excess such as flushing, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Hemochromatosis (Choice C) results in excessive iron levels and presents with hepatic, cardiac, and renal failure in addition to hyperpigmentation. Hyperthyroidism (Choice D) can present with weight loss, hair loss, tachycardia, tachypnea, diarrhea, diaphoresis, and muscle wasting and weakness, however it is not as likely a cause as lung cancer in a cachectic patient who smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years.

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue over the past 6 months. She has had a decreased appetite and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss over the past year. She has not had nausea or vomiting, abdominal pain, changes in bowel movements, diarrhea, or blood in the stool. She has a 2-year history of pruritus. She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. She has no known allergies. Her mother has Graves disease, her sister has systemic lupus erythematosus, and a paternal uncle has hemochromatosis. Her pulse is 80/min and regular, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/85 mm Hg. Examination shows excoriations over the upper and lower extremities and trunk with no lesions. There are xanthomas around the eyelids. Abdominal examination shows a liver span of 12 cm; there are no palpable masses or tenderness. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, Leukocyte count 3500/mm3, Platelet count 100,000/mm3, Serum Cholesterol 350 mg/dL, Total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, Alkaline phosphatase 450 U/L, AST 30 U/L, ALT 35 U/L. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows hepatomegaly and no evidence of a biliary obstruction. There is a large gallstone in the gallbladder and mild splenomegaly. Which of the following is most likely to suggest the diagnosis?

choices.C: Serum hepatitis B surface antigen and antibody and core antibody assays

correctExplanation: Primary biliary cirrhosis is an autoimmune disease of the biliary tree resulting in destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts. It often affects middle-aged women. Because of disordered biliary excretion, it classically presents with jaundice, pruritus, hypercholesterolemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies. It is associated with a positive serum antimitochondrial antibody, although biopsy is needed for definitive diagnosis. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line therapy, improving biliary excretion, but liver transplantation may be necessary in progressive, severe disease.
incorrectExplanation: B, C, D, E, and F. Serum antinuclear antibody assay (Choice B) is elevated in many autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. It is classically a sensitive test for systemic lupus erythematosus. Serum hepatitis B surface antigen assay (Choice C) is used to identify active or chronic hepatitis B infection, which, if acute, classically presents with nausea, vomiting, anorexia, hepatomegaly, and jaundice, with elevated transaminase levels. Oral cholecystography (Choice D) and HIDA scan (Choice E) are used to evaluate the gallbladder, which, when inflamed or obstructed, presents with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, or diarrhea. This patient is symptomatic with multiple biliary laboratory abnormalities (eg, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase), and, therefore, further diagnostic steps are required to guide therapy (Choice F).

questionStem: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician 1 day after noticing pink-tinged urine. Two days ago, he had an upper respiratory tract infection with a nonproductive, hacking cough; his symptoms are now resolved. He has not had pain, fever, or chills. He has no history of serious illness. Current medications include over-the-counter cough syrup. He does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 114/68 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows a pH of 5.5, 4+ blood, and greater than 50 RBC/hpf. His serum creatinine concentration is 1.1 mg/dL, and serum complement concentration is within the reference range. Ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Correct Answer: B. IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is a type of nephritic syndrome resulting in episodic gross hematuria often following an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. On urinalysis, there will be a significant quantity of red blood cells (RBCs) and the possibility for RBC cast formation. Serum complement levels, including C3, are typically normal, which differentiates IgA nephropathy from postinfectious glomerulonephritis, which results in low serum C3 complement. Additionally, anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers will be negative in IgA nephropathy.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Cystitis (Choice A) refers to inflammation of the urinary bladder, which most commonly is secondary to an acute bacterial urinary tract infection. A typical infectious cystitis presents with increased urinary white blood cells, with elevated leukocyte esterase and possibly elevated nitrites depending on the infectious organism. It does not typically follow an upper respiratory infection, and hematuria may be variably present. Nongonococcal urethritis (Choice C) is typically secondary to infection from Chlamydia trachomatis and presents with characteristic findings on gram stain of numerous neutrophils but no bacteria (sterile pyuria). Postinfectious glomerulonephritis (Choice D) is a nephritic syndrome presenting with urinary RBCs and RBC casts, which typically occurs 2-6 weeks after infection with group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. On laboratory examination, it demonstrates low serum C3 levels, and positive anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers. Renal cell carcinoma (Choice E) is an adenocarcinoma of tubular epithelial cells. Patients may present with gross hematuria (without RBC casts), flank pain, and possible palpable flank mass. Diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma typically occurs with contrast-enhanced CT or MRI and is confirmed by biopsy at the time of nephrectomy.

questionStem: An 82-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is brought to the emergency department by his children because he has been unresponsive for the past 24 hours. His family reports that he has become increasingly sleepy and confused over the past 2 weeks. His lung cancer was diagnosed 3 years ago and initially treated with palliative radiation therapy to his chest and right femur. Nine months ago, he and his oncologist agreed to discontinue treatment. He has had a 16-kg (35-lb) weight loss over the past 9 months. He has lived in his son's house for the past 6 months and has received palliative care only. The patient has an advance directive indicating that he does not want lifesaving treatment, and the son has stated that his father recently confirmed these wishes verbally. His daughter, who lives out of state, disagrees with the plan to provide palliative care at home only and is concerned about her father's weight loss. After a family meeting, both siblings now request that the physician switch to an aggressive treatment plan. The patient appears cachectic but well groomed. He responds to painful stimuli only. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 52 kg (115 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m2. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 34/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 85/50 mm Hg. Serum studies show: Na+ 142 mEq/L, Ca2+ 13.2 mg/dL, Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, Albumin 3 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.D: Perform lifesaving measures until the family issues can be resolved

correctExplanation: Advance directives are formal specifications of a patient's wishes, created and executed during a time of decision-making capacity. They are enacted when the patient loses capacity to communicate preferences about healthcare wishes. Often, these documents govern end-of-life care, and are commonly used in cases of terminal illness, with late-stage malignancy a very common time of use. Advance directives should reflect a patient's wishes as expressed during periods of stable values and preferences, and the medicolegal strength of an advance directive is greater when family members or persons who know the patient corroborate the document's accurate reflection of long-standing and stable wishes. In this case, this patient had an advance directive written and prepared for use in such a case, and his son, who lives locally and seems to know the patient and his preferences, corroborates what his father would have wanted. Following the advance directive is the most appropriate course of action, while showing compassion and empathy to the family.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, D, and E. Contacting the hospital attorney (Choice A) or ethics committee (Choice B) is unnecessary. The patient's wishes are clearly stated in his advance directive, and there is no evidence that the patient's wishes for himself have changed since the time of drafting and execution. The patient has clearly stated that he does not want lifesaving measures (Choice D), and he and his oncology team had also agreed that aggressive care (Choice E) would be futile given the extent and aggressive nature of his malignancy.

questionStem: A 42-year-old African American woman comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of cough and fatigue. She has long-standing hypertension well controlled with atenolol. Her blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Serum studies show: Ca2+ 11.8 mg/dL, Phosphorus 3.4 mg/dL, Globulin 4.8 g/dL, Parathyroid hormone, intact 7 pg/mL (N=10–65), Parathyroid hormone-related protein 1.0 pmol/L (N<1.3). An x-ray of the chest shows several nodules throughout both lung fields. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Sarcoidosis is an immune-mediated systemic disease resulting in formation of noncaseating granulomas in a variety of involved organs. It is most common in African American females and is often asymptomatic except for lymphadenopathy, with radiographs potentially demonstrating bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and reticulonodular opacities of bilateral lungs. Granulomatous inflammation can result in autonomous production of 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxy-vitamin D3 to the active form 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D3. This granulomatous expression of the enzyme results in an increased production of active vitamin D3, which leads to increased intestinal absorption of calcium, resulting in hypercalcemia. This vitamin D3-dependent hypercalcemia results in physiologic suppression of parathyroid hormone. Glucocorticoids are the first-line therapy for sarcoidosis, which are utilized to suppress the granulomatous inflammation characteristic of the disease.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, E, F, and G. Calcitriol (Choice A) refers to the active form of 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D3, which would worsen this patient's hypercalcemia. Divalproex sodium (Choice B) is used in the treatment of seizures, migraine headaches, and psychiatric disturbances such as bipolar disorder. Gallium nitrate (Choice C) treats symptomatic cancer-associated hypercalcemia through inhibition of osteoclast activity. Plicamycin (Choice E) inhibits RNA synthesis, serving as an anti-neoplastic antibiotic, and is rarely used for the treatment of hypercalcemia. Dialysis (Choice F) is utilized for the removal of excess solutes, toxins, and/or water from patients in emergent settings of acute renal failure or chronic end-stage renal disease. Dialysis may be indicated in cases of severe hypercalcemia, where native renal clearance mechanisms will be insufficient or inappropriately slow. Parathyroidectomy (Choice G) is indicated for the treatment of hypercalcemia caused by primary hyperparathyroidism.

questionStem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of shortness of breath on exertion over the past 2 weeks. His last examination was 38 years ago. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is not increased. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. Cardiac examination shows an S4 gallop. Pulses are symmetric without bruits. There is no peripheral edema. His fasting serum glucose concentration is 130 mg/dL, and fasting serum cholesterol concentration is 270 mg/dL. An x-ray of the chest shows mild cardiomegaly and Kerley B lines. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiography shows a thickened left ventricle and an ejection fraction of 40% without segmental wall abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented the echocardiographic findings?

choices.B: Adequate control of serum glucose concentrations

correctExplanation: Hypertension is a common cause of chronic systolic and diastolic left-sided heart failure and is considered a modifiable risk factor. This patient’s history, signs, symptoms, and exam findings are consistent with chronic left-sided heart failure. Given the lack of an elevated jugular venous pulse, it is unlikely the patient has developed right-sided heart failure. On echocardiography, the patient has a reduced ejection fraction, indicative of systolic heart failure. On physical exam, there is an S4 gallop with evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy on electrocardiogram, which indicates diastolic heart failure. Additionally, his chest x-ray demonstrates evidence of pulmonary edema (eg, Kerley B lines), a consequence of left-sided heart failure. Adequate control of blood pressure decreases afterload and reduces the degree of cardiac myocyte hypertrophy, which decreases the risk of developing heart failure.
incorrectExplanation: B, C, D, and E. Adequate control of serum glucose (Choice B) reduces the risk of microvascular complications of diabetes mellitus, such as retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. Evidence for tight glucose control as a means of significantly reducing macrovascular complications from diabetes mellitus is less clear. Beta-adrenergic agonist therapy (Choice C) is the appropriate treatment for obstructive lung disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or moderate persistent asthma. Low-cholesterol diet (Choice D) would assist in the treatment of hypercholesterolemia, a modifiable risk factor, reducing the likelihood of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. This would reduce his risk for coronary artery disease, with a less direct impact on his risk for developing chronic heart failure. Smoking cessation (Choice E) is a modifiable risk factor in the reduction of cardiovascular and pulmonary disease, although uncontrolled hypertension imparts greater relative risk in this case.

questionStem: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of severe chest pressure and nausea. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He has smoked three packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He is employed as a truck driver and has a sedentary lifestyle. He appears anxious and diaphoretic. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 107 kg (235 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2. His pulse is 44/min and regular, and blood pressure is 160/94 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Peripheral pulses are normal. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cardiac rhythm?
correctExplanation: Complete heart block is characterized on an ECG by complete dissociation of P waves from the QRS complex. This ECG shows an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The inferior wall of the heart and the atrioventricular (AV) node often share a common blood supply from the right coronary artery (RCA). When the RCA is blocked, infarction of both the inferior wall and the AV node can occur, which can lead to an AV block with a junctional escape rhythm. In normal sinus rhythm, there is a one-to-one relationship between the P wave and QRS complex, which is not seen in the setting of complete heart block. In fact, there is no relationship between the P and QRS frequencies, with each maintaining its own unique, separate rate per minute. This ECG shows an escape rhythm; the R-R interval is constant and the QRS complex is narrow suggesting a pacer focus located in the common bundle or just distal to the AV node within the His-Purkinje system.
incorrectExplanation: B, C, D, and E. First-degree atrioventricular block (Choice B) results in a prolonged P-R interval, defined as greater than 200 milliseconds. While this ECG shows some PR intervals greater than 200 milliseconds, the absence of a consistent P-QRS relationship indicates complete heart block. Mobitz type I (Wenckebach type) block (Choice C) is diagnosed when the PR interval progressively lengthens, resulting in a non-conducted beat and resultant absence of the corresponding QRS. Following a short pause, the cycle begins again, resulting in a phenomenon on ECG known as “grouped beating.” Mobitz type II block (Choice D) is seen as a consistent P-R interval; however, a number of normal beats are followed by a dropped QRS (a non-conducted P wave). This occurs in a discrete ratio, often three-to-two or two-to-one. Sinus bradycardia (Choice E) is characterized by a one-to-one ratio of P to QRS, with a ventricular rate less than 60 beats per minute.

questionStem: A previously healthy 25-year-old graduate student comes to the physician because of numbness of her left leg, stiffness of her right leg, and urinary urgency. Examination shows increased tone and deep tendon reflexes in the right lower extremity. Babinski sign is present on the right. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the left lower extremity and below the level of T9 on the left. Sensation to vibration and proprioception is intact. Gait testing shows stiffness and circumduction of the right lower extremity. This patient is most likely to have a lesion at which of the following locations?
correctExplanation: A lesion within the spinal cord can result in injury to a single or multiple spinal cord tracts. This can lead to asymmetric physical exam findings depending on the location of the lesion. Fine touch (pinprick) and temperature are transmitted by the anterolateral spinothalamic (ALS) tract. Motor function is carried along the lateral corticospinal tract (CST). Sensation of vibration and proprioception are transmitted along the dorsal columns-medial lemniscus pathway (DC-ML). A lesion located within the anterior and lateral fascicles of the spinal cord white matter would result in injury to the ALS tract and lateral CST. This would result in contralateral loss of fine touch and temperature perception since the primary sensory neuron for the ALS tract decussates within the spinal cord along the ventral white commissure, followed by ascent within the anterolateral tract of the spinal cord. Additionally, there would be findings of ipsilateral motor weakness as motor decussation occurs in the brain stem.
