With injury to the lateral CST, the patient would manifest upper motoneuron exam findings such as spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and E. Lesions within the brain stem (Choice A) typically result in ipsilateral loss of cranial nerve function (variable depending on the location within the brain stem) and contralateral loss of long-tract spinal cord function (ie, CST, ALS, or DC-ML). For example, a lesion within the lateral medulla results in Wallenberg syndrome, manifesting with ipsilateral loss of sensation to the face and contralateral body, along with additional cranial nerve symptomatology such as dysphagia, hoarseness, and decreased gag reflex. A lesion within the cerebral hemisphere (Choice B) would result in a contralateral focal neurologic deficit dependent on the location of the lesion. Lesions within the cerebral hemisphere do not result in bilateral asymmetric neurologic exam findings. Peripheral nerve lesions (Choice C) result in symptoms (lower motoneuron weakness, paresthesias, and numbness) within a specific dermatome or peripheral nerve distribution (eg, radial nerve). Conversion reaction (Choice E), also referred to as functional neurologic symptom disorder, can result in loss of motor or sensory function that cannot be explained by a physical illness or injury. Patients are often aware of the symptoms but indifferent about their significance ('la belle indifference').

questionStem: A 38-year-old African American man with accelerated hypertension is admitted to the hospital. His blood pressure is 230/130 mm Hg and he has grade III retinopathy. Serum creatinine concentration is 3.7 mg/dL. Antihypertensive therapy is begun. Twenty-four hours later he develops oliguria, and 5 days later his serum creatinine concentration increases to 6.8 mg/dL. He has substernal chest pain and a pericardial friction rub. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of the pericardial disease?
correctExplanation: Uremia can present with nausea, asterixis, encephalopathy, platelet dysfunction, and pericarditis. This patient's presentation is consistent with uremic pericarditis in the setting of acute renal failure, as a result of uncontrolled hypertension. Accelerated hypertension (now known as hypertensive emergency) is defined as an abrupt, significant increase in blood pressure resulting in end-organ damage. The brain, retina, heart, vasculature, and kidneys are commonly affected, in this case reflected by vision changes in the setting of acute hypertension. Acutely increased blood pressure can result in end-organ damage to the kidney secondary to glomerular and arteriolar injury, which can sometimes be worsened by abrupt antihypertensive therapy. If severe enough, oliguria with an associated rise in serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen can result, leading to symptoms and signs of uremia.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and E. Collagen vascular disease (Choice A) relates to systemic genetic and autoimmune connective tissue diseases such as Alport syndrome, systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Marfan syndrome, or Ehlers Danlos syndrome. All of these conditions would be expected to present with a different constellation of symptoms, some of which have the potential for acute renal failure, but typically this is superimposed on the chronic disease state. Pericarditis related to an infection is common, although this patient demonstrates neither signs of infection nor preceding history (eg, fever, viral prodrome) making pyogenic infection (Choice B), tuberculosis (Choice C), and viral infection (Choice E) unlikely, especially given the temporal relation of the patient's accelerated hypertension to renal failure and pericarditis.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine follow-up examination. She has mild, intermittent asthma treated with an albuterol inhaler as needed. During the past 3 weeks, she has had three to four weekly episodes of shortness of breath and wheezing that resolve with use of the inhaler. She has never required intubation for asthma. She is otherwise asymptomatic. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications. There are no known sick contacts. Her temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/64 mm Hg. Wheezes are heard bilaterally. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

choices.A: Increase the dosage of albuterol to four times daily

correctExplanation: Asthma is characterized by reversible obstruction of the bronchi secondary to hyperreactivity and airway inflammation. Patients present with episodes of wheezing, dry cough, and dyspnea. On physical examination, wheezes are heard, and there is sometimes a component of prolonged expiration relative to inspiration. Chest radiographs are typically normal. Pulmonary function tests may be normal between symptomatic exacerbations but during such episodes demonstrate an obstructive pattern with increased residual volume and total lung capacity. The severity of asthma is graded based on frequency of day- and night-time symptomatic episodes. Intermittent asthma is characterized as symptoms occurring ≤2 days per week and ≤2 nights per month and requires as-needed short-acting bronchodilators for symptomatic relief. Individuals with mild persistent asthma (such as this patient) exhibit symptoms >2 days per week or >2 nights per month, which requires the addition of daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroids (eg, fluticasone). Moderate persistent asthma is treated with the addition of long-acting inhaled beta-2 agonists (eg, salmeterol) to the regimen of low-dose inhaled corticosteroids and as-needed short-acting bronchodilator. Severe persistent asthma is treated with the addition of high-dose corticosteroids to the regimen.
incorrectExplanation: Albuterol inhalers (Choice A) act as stand-alone treatment for intermittent asthma to assist in shortening symptomatic exacerbations. While albuterol plays a role in the management of all types of asthma, her asthma is mild persistent and requires the addition of a steroid. Salmeterol (Choice C) is a long-acting beta-2 agonist, used in treatment of moderate persistent asthma, working in conjunction with low-dose inhaled corticosteroids. Theophylline (Choice D) results in bronchodilation through the inhibition of phosphodiesterase. It has a narrow therapeutic window, resulting in significant cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity. It is a late and/or last-line treatment. Tiotropium (Choice E) is a long-acting anti-muscarinic agent resulting in bronchodilation, which is indicated for use in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

questionStem: During transfusion of a second unit of crossmatched packed red blood cells for lower gastrointestinal bleeding, a 67-year-old woman has the onset of fever and chills. Six months ago, she had gastrointestinal bleeding and had no complications after transfusion of 3 units of crossmatched packed red blood cells. She appears anxious. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), pulse is 105/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 135/75 mm Hg. Examination of the skin shows no abnormalities. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Serum studies of a post-transfusion sample show no free hemoglobin. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative. The ABO blood groups of the patient and donor are verified, and a second crossmatch reconfirms compatibility. In addition to intravenous administration of crystalloid solution, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Correct Answer: A. Acute febrile transfusion reactions occur during the administration of blood transfusions secondary to preformed cytokines in the transfused blood. This reaction is not related to inaccurate cross-matching or administration of an incorrect blood type to the patient. It is treated with acetaminophen plus fluids to blunt the hypothalamic response to cytokines. In contrast, hemolytic transfusion reactions would present with a positive Coombs test and free hemoglobin in serum.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Dantrolene (Choice B) is commonly used to treat malignant hyperthermia, which is characterized by rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability, often due to anesthetic medications or nitrates. Epinephrine (Choice C) is used to treat anaphylactic transfusion reactions which would be characterized by tachycardia, wheezing, hypotension, angioedema, itching, urticaria, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Penicillin (Choice D) is an antibiotic used to treat various gram-positive and spirochete infections. In the setting of a fever occurring during a transfusion, the time course is likely too abrupt to reflect a new infection, even if acquired from the blood. Prednisone (Choice E) is used to treat multiple inflammatory, atopic, infectious, and autoimmune conditions. It has no specific role in managing an acute febrile transfusion reaction.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of fatigue, heat intolerance, generalized anxiety, and intermittent palpitations; she has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss during this period. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. Her pulse is 104/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 112/78 mm Hg. Examination shows a 2-cm, discrete, firm nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid gland. There is no cervical adenopathy. Her serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is less than 0.3 μU/mL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.B: Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid gland
choices.C: Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid gland
choices.E: Toxic adenoma of the thyroid gland

correctExplanation: Correct Answer: E. Hyperthyroidism is characterized by symptoms and signs, including but not limited to heat intolerance, generalized anxiety, palpitations, weight loss, hair loss, sweating, diarrhea, amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea, and tachycardia. On physical examination, there is often a discrete, single palpable thyroid nodule, multiple nodules, or diffuse enlargement of the gland depending on the etiology. This patient has a low TSH, confirming the presence of primary hyperthyroidism, and the presence of a nodule on exam in this setting is strongly suggestive of a solitary, hyperfunctioning toxic adenoma.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and F. Graves disease (Choice A) results from the inappropriate production of thyroid-stimulating antibodies. The parenchyma of the gland is diffusely stimulated via this antibody, which has a trophic effect and results in global, as opposed to focal, enlargement of the gland. Medullary (Choice B) and papillary carcinoma (Choice C) of the thyroid result in palpable nodules, however, would typically be nonfunctional, resulting in a euthyroid state or hypothyroidism depending on the size of the lesion. Riedel thyroiditis (Choice D) is characterized by chronic, invasive fibrosis of the thyroid. It can transiently present with symptoms of hyperthyroidism early in the disease but more often presents with chronic hypothyroidism as gland parenchyma becomes replaced by nonfunctional stroma. Toxic multinodular goiter (Choice F) presents with symptoms of hyperthyroidism and multiple palpable nodules as opposed to a single nodule.

questionStem: An 87-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of constant, increasing abdominal pain. The pain is not related to eating. She has had generalized itching for the past week. She underwent a cholecystectomy for gallstones at the age of 63 years. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 79 kg (175 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 142/82 mm Hg. Examination shows excoriations on both upper extremities. Abdominal examination shows mild epigastric tenderness. Results of a complete blood count are within the reference range. Serum studies show: Total bilirubin 1.9 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase 305 U/L AST 34 U/L ALT 42 U/L Amylase 56 U/L Abdominal ultrasonography shows dilation of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct. The pancreas is poorly visualized because of overlying bowel gas. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma most commonly occurs in the pancreatic head. It is often initially characterized by nonspecific vague abdominal discomfort or weight loss. As the pancreatic mass increases in size, it can lead to the obstruction and dilation of both the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct, referred to as a double-duct sign on ultrasound. This can result in painless jaundice and/or pancreatitis from obstruction of these ducts. If the pancreatic adenocarcinoma continues to spread and results in infiltration of surrounding abdominal viscera and/or encasement of adjacent neurovascular structures, this can manifest with severe abdominal pain. The nonspecific nature of pancreatic adenocarcinoma's early symptoms creates a diagnostic dilemma, as many benign conditions present similarly. It is frequently asymptomatic until it creates an obstruction, gastrointestinal dysfunction, perineural or vascular encasement/invasion, or metastatic disease.
incorrectExplanation: A, C, D, and E. Choledocholithiasis (Choice A) presents with acute right upper quadrant and epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting, often following a fatty meal in a patient with either known gallstones or risk factors for them. This patient had a cholecystectomy and while post-cholecystectomy syndromes including ductal stones are possible, they are less likely. Primary biliary cirrhosis (Choice C) results in destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts and classically presents in middle-aged females. It is characterized by jaundice, pruritus, anorexia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Sclerosing cholangitis (Choice D) presents either primarily or in patients with a history of ulcerative colitis. It presents as inflammation and chronic fibrosis of the biliary tree resulting in a beaded appearance to the biliary tree with multifocal strictures. Symptoms of sclerosing cholangitis include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and malabsorption. Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (Choice E) would result in dilated biliary and pancreatic ducts on imaging; however, this would be transient and not necessarily accompanied by an elevation in alkaline phosphatase or additional symptoms such as pain and itching.

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-month history of progressive shortness of breath, cough, and intermittent wheezing. Her cough usually is nonproductive but occasionally has produced white sputum. She is otherwise asymptomatic. Nine months ago, she was intubated and mechanically ventilated for 2 weeks for management of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Her only medication is a daily multivitamin. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. She smokes marijuana two times monthly. She does not drink alcohol. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. High-pitched, end-expiratory wheezes are heard in the anterior aspect of the lungs. No crackles are heard. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: E. Tracheomalacia refers to softening and deterioration of the tracheal cartilage, which results in excessive end-expiratory collapse due to atrophy and/or reduction of the tracheal elastic fibers and decreased integrity of tracheal cartilage. In adults, this most commonly occurs after prolonged intubation with an endotracheal tube, which results in damage to the tracheal cartilage directly, and can increase the risk of tracheomalacia. Clinically, this presents with shortness of breath, nonproductive cough, and expiratory stridor. It can also sound like wheezing on lung auscultation.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and D. The patient has a recent history of prolonged intubation, with no reported prior history of asthma (Choice A). Her high-pitched, end-expiratory wheezes and other symptoms are likely secondary to tracheomalacia and its associated expiratory collapse. Guillain-Barré syndrome (Choice B) is typically self-limited and affects the lungs through diaphragmatic paralysis, not through an obstructive airway mechanism as seen in this patient. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Choice C) results in shortness of breath, cough, and fever after exposure to a specific antigen. Paradoxic vocal cord motion (Choice D) occurs when the vocal cords close during breathing, resulting in an obstructed airway. There are many causes of paradoxic vocal cord motion, including exercise, coughing, and acid reflux.

questionStem: A 47-year-old woman with hypertension comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. One month ago, her blood pressure was 200/120 mm Hg, and daily treatment with an oral ACE inhibitor was started. Examination at that visit showed no other abnormalities, and results of serum electrolyte concentrations and renal function studies were within the reference range. Her blood pressure today is 170/90 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Her serum creatinine concentration is 2.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Addition of thiazide diuretic therapy to the current regimen
choices.D: Increase in the dose of ACE inhibitor
choices.E: MR angiography of the renal arteries

correctExplanation: This patient presents with a significant rise in creatinine following initiation of an ACE inhibitor for hypertension management. ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II production, which can lead to a significant reduction in renal blood flow if an existing renal artery stenosis is present. This reduction in blood flow to the kidneys, if bilateral, can result in a prerenal acute kidney injury, which manifests as a rise in creatinine following administration of the ACE inhibitor. To diagnose the patient's probable renal artery stenosis, CT or MR angiography can outline the renal artery anatomy to guide therapy.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and D. Measurement of plasma renin activity or urine catecholamine concentration (Choices A and B) would be indicated if symptoms suggestive of secondary hypertension due to elevations in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system or due to a pheochromocytoma, respectively, were present. A second medication may be necessary to control this patient's hypertension (Choice C), but a renovascular cause of hypertension must be addressed before determining the appropriate medication regimen. Increasing the dose of ACE inhibitor (Choice D) is inappropriate at this time since it would likely worsen renal function in the setting of renal artery stenosis.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a lesion on the calf for 2 months. A photograph of the lesion is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: A nevus of the skin is more likely to be a malignancy such as melanoma when it demonstrates asymmetry, irregular borders, uneven coloring, diameter ≥6 mm, and rapid evolution. Appropriate management of a potentially malignant dermatologic lesion consists of excision with negative margins, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. This is performed either through minimally invasive surgery such as Mohs, or through a wider traditional surgical excision.
incorrectExplanation: Corticosteroid therapy (Choice A) would be appropriate if this lesion were inflammatory or atopic (eg, eczema). Antibiotic therapy (Choice B) would be appropriate for an infectious lesion (eg, cellulitis, erysipelas). This lesion is more likely malignant given its concerning features, and these therapies would delay definitive diagnosis and treatment, increasing the risk for distant and lymph node metastases. Cryotherapy (Choice C) with liquid nitrogen is indicated for premalignant lesions, such as actinic keratosis, or hyperkeratotic lesions, such as condylomas (warts). Punch biopsy (Choice D) would provide diagnostic information but would not be therapeutic, since a portion of the lesion is left behind, and negative margins would not be confirmed. This lesion shows several concerning features for an aggressive malignancy, which must be diagnosed and treated (Choice F).

questionStem: A 77-year-old man with dementia, Alzheimer type, is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of urinary incontinence. He has had frequent loss of small amounts of urine, especially at night. Abdominal examination shows tenderness and a 10-cm tender suprapubic mass. He can void spontaneously and has a poor urinary stream. Urinalysis shows 4 WBC/hpf and 1+ bacteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

choices.C: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

correctExplanation: Urinary retention, nighttime overflow incontinence, and a weak urinary stream are characteristic of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in older men, which can lead to bladder outlet obstruction. The best next step to relieve a bladder outlet obstruction involves catheterization to decompress the urinary bladder and prevent acute complications of prolonged bladder outlet obstruction such as bladder rupture, urothelial cell atrophy or necrosis, hydronephrosis, postrenal azotemia, and/or renal failure.
incorrectExplanation: Observation (Choice A) is inappropriate as this patient presents with a bladder outlet obstruction that must be managed to prevent further complications. X-rays of the abdomen (Choice B), and CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (Choice C) may provide diagnostic information but would not play a role in the immediate management of bladder outlet obstruction from BPH. The urinalysis indicates the presence of bacteriuria, but the patient's symptoms are from BPH and bladder obstruction and are not typical for a urinary tract infection. Asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated with antibiotic therapy (Choice D) unless the patient is pregnant, or the patient's urinary tract has recently been manipulated for a urologic procedure.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination. He feels well. He has rheumatoid arthritis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications include methotrexate, metformin, lisinopril, simvastatin, and 81-mg aspirin. He drinks one to two glasses of wine each evening. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg. Examination shows an abdominal bruit. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ 142 mEq/L, K+ 3.5 mEq/L, Cl- 120 mEq/L, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, Glucose 134 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, Urine pH 6.5. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) results in a hyperchloremic, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from dysregulation of the renal tubules. There are three types of RTA, varying in etiology and pathophysiology, but all resulting in a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. This patient demonstrates a low bicarbonate level, with a normal anion gap of 12, consistent with a non-anion gap acidosis. Distal RTA (type 1) results from a defect in renal secretion of H+, which results in the lack of generation of HCO3-; ultimately leading to a metabolic acidosis. It is characterized by a urine pH >5.5. The most common causes of type 1 RTA include analgesic nephropathy, congenital obstructive urinary tract anomalies, drugs (eg, amphotericin), and autoimmune diseases resulting in hypergammaglobulinemia (eg, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren).
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and E. Alcohol use (Choice A) does not independently alter acid-base pathology outside of extremes such as alcoholic ketoacidosis or consumption of volatile alcohols that are metabolized to organic acids such as methanol and ethylene glycol. Diabetic ketoacidosis (Choice B) typically occurs in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus as a result of increased insulin requirements during times of physiologic stress (eg, infection) or insulin nonadherence. Diabetic ketoacidosis results in a metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. Increased lactate production (Choice C) can result from any hypoperfusion state, deficiency in the TCA cycle, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, or from vitamin deficiencies (eg, thiamine), and is associated with an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. Salicylate intoxication (Choice E) initially results in the development of respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation with a delayed anion gap metabolic acidosis.

questionStem: A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing for 6 days. He says that food becomes stuck in his throat. Over the past 2 weeks, he has had low-grade fever and fatigue. He has had an 11-kg (25-lb) weight loss over the past year. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He uses intravenous heroin. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 110/78 mm Hg. Examination shows anterior and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. There are thick white plaques over the buccal mucosa and soft palate. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's dysphagia?
correctExplanation: C. Dysphagia has many structural, malignant, neurologic, infectious, and inflammatory causes. In the setting of weight loss, fatigue, low-grade fever, and intravenous drug abuse, the white oropharyngeal plaques are consistent with esophagitis from Candida species as a cause of dysphagia, a common opportunistic infection in an immunocompromised host such as a person with HIV. The patient's cervical lymphadenopathy is likely reactive to the adjacent esophageal infectious process. Herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus are also common infectious etiologies of esophagitis in this population, but these typically present with esophageal ulcers.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E. Bacterial endocarditis (Choice A) presents classically with fevers, a new heart murmur, evidence of disseminated infection such as septic emboli, and vascular/immunologic phenomena such as Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, and splinter hemorrhages. Esophageal cancer with nodal metastases (Choice B) could explain the patient's dysphagia, weight loss, and vague systemic symptoms, however, would not classically present with white oropharyngeal plaques, but rather esophageal narrowing with irregular borders from an infiltrative neoplastic mass. Oral cancer with nodal metastases (Choice D) could present with a white oral plaque (eg, squamous cell carcinoma); however, this would typically be a solitary plaque as opposed to multiple, thick plaques. Tertiary syphilis (Choice E) would not be expected to present with multiple white oral plaques; it classically presents with neurologic symptoms, gummas, and aortitis.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-hour history of shortness of breath and nonproductive cough. She has had similar episodes, which typically last 18 hours, two to three times weekly during the past 3 months. She is asymptomatic when she runs outside for 45 minutes, five times weekly. She has not had chest pain. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is an oral contraceptive. She does not smoke cigarettes. She smokes marijuana once monthly. She moved to a new apartment building 4 months ago and she often uses the communal pool and hot tub. She appears to be in mild respiratory distress. Her temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. She is not using accessory muscles of respiration. Diffuse, fine crackles are heard prominently at the lung bases; no wheezes are heard. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis represents a mixed type III and IV hypersensitivity reaction to various environmental antigens. This typically results in episodic dyspnea, fever, and cough which starts a few hours after the exposure to the antigen. Classically, this occurs in farmers and individuals exposed to bird droppings. It can also occur secondary to the use of hot tubs and resultant antigen exposure, as seen in this patient. Similarly, her symptoms may also represent a chemical pneumonitis or bronchitis from inhaled chlorine. Treatment requires avoidance of the specific inciting antigen. If chronic exposure occurs, this can result in alveolar thickening, noncaseating granuloma formation, and possible upper lobe predominant pulmonary fibrosis.
incorrectExplanation: Contraceptives (Choice A), if primarily estrogen based, may increase the risk of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Pulmonary embolism typically presents with acute-onset chest pain and shortness of breath and would less likely be episodic as in this patient. Illicit drug use (Choice C) may result in various degrees of shortness of breath depending on the agent and mode of use. Marijuana, when smoked, can result in tracheobronchial inflammation and/or pneumonitis, although she only smokes once monthly, which does not correlate with the frequency of her symptoms. Swimming pool use (Choice D) is not directly associated with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, though could be associated with a chemical pneumonitis from chlorine. The type of exercise (Choice E) may have an impact on a patient's asthma symptoms, although would not play a role in hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

questionStem: A 32-year-old homeless man is admitted to the hospital and placed in respiratory isolation because of a 2-week history of fever, chills, and cough productive of blood-tinged sputum. He also has had shortness of breath after walking approximately 100 feet. He has had a 13.6-kg (30-lb) weight loss during the past 6 months. He takes no prescription medications but has a history of intravenous drug use. He is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 45 kg (100 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m2. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. He is using accessory muscles of respiration. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Examination shows shotty cervical lymphadenopathy. There is bilateral wasting of the temporal and supraclavicular muscles. Diffuse crackles are heard throughout both lung fields. His leukocyte count is 11,500/mm3 (70% segmented neutrophils, 1% eosinophils, 1% basophils, 25% lymphocytes, and 3% monocytes). A PPD skin test is negative. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis can present in various stages. Primary tuberculosis results from an initial exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, leading to the development of hilar lymphadenopathy and a Ghon focus (Ghon complex). Reactivation tuberculosis (secondary) typically results in apical pulmonary opacity with fibrocaseous cavitary lesions. This may present clinically with prolonged fever, night sweats, weight loss (including skeletal muscle wasting), and hemoptysis. A PPD skin test can be negative in the setting of tuberculosis infection if the patient is immunocompromised. Reactivation tuberculosis requires combination anti-microbial treatment including rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, along with initial respiratory isolation.
incorrectExplanation: Aspiration pneumonia (Choice A) occurs in patients at risk for aspiration (eg, elderly, stroke, dementia). It commonly presents with cough and fever following an aspiration episode, with consolidation most commonly occurring in the dependent portions of the right middle or lower lobes. Bronchiectasis (Choice B) refers to chronic dilation of the bronchi and/or bronchioles as a result of chronic necrotizing infection, most commonly related to chronic bronchial obstruction, cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Sarcoidosis (Choice C) is a chronic non-caseating granulomatous systemic inflammatory condition, which most commonly affects the hilar lymph nodes and lungs. Pulmonary sarcoidosis can result in coarse reticular pulmonary opacities, which may progress to a restrictive lung disease from interstitial fibrosis, although acute fever and hemoptysis would be rare. Septic pulmonary emboli (Choice D) typically occur in the setting of endocarditis (eg, tricuspid valve) or infected sources of the venous system (eg, Lemierre syndrome). Wegener granulomatosis (Choice F) can result in multifocal cavitary pulmonary nodules, but typically also occurs in the setting of upper respiratory tract symptoms (eg, perforated nasal septum, chronic sinusitis) and glomerulonephritis (eg, hematuria).

questionStem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician for a health maintenance examination. She has mild hyperparathyroidism that does not require treatment. She takes no medications. She does not exercise or eat meat or dairy products. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 104 kg (230 lb); BMI is 40 kg/m2. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for osteoarthritis in this patient during the next 10 years?
correctExplanation: Osteoarthritis is a noninflammatory arthropathy secondary to deterioration of articular cartilage, often related to multifactorial etiologies with an interplay of systemic and local factors. Obesity is one of the most common risk factors for the development of osteoarthritis. Excess weight results in consistent, increased daily joint stress and degradation of the articular cartilage. Further, humoral factors from adipose cells plus leptin system derangements cause alterations in metabolism of articular cartilage. These factors result in an increased rate of degradation.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and E. Calcium deficiency (Choice A), hyperparathyroidism (Choice B), and Vitamin D deficiency (Choice E) increase the risk for osteoporosis secondary to demineralization. Hypocalcemia has been shown to be associated with knee osteoarthritis, although less than obesity. Vitamin D deficiency can result in clinically significant hypocalcemia. Vitamin D deficiency as an independent cause of osteoarthritis has not been clearly established but may contribute to articular cartilage degeneration. Hyperparathyroidism can lead to the development of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) with the development of chondrocalcinosis but is not related to noninflammatory osteoarthritis. A lack of exercise (Choice C) does not directly increase the risk of osteoarthritis, although this may be a surrogate marker of a patient’s general daily activities and risk for developing excess weight.

questionStem: A 47-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for treatment of alcoholic pancreatitis. He is currently receiving intravenous 0.9% saline, intravenous morphine, oral lorazepam for alcohol withdrawal, and multiple vitamins. He has no known allergies. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. He drinks one fifth of vodka daily. He frequently has sexual intercourse with prostitutes. On examination, he is diaphoretic. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/84 mm Hg. Examination shows no lymphadenopathy. The abdomen is distended with epigastric tenderness. A photograph of the genitalia is shown. There is a lesion under the prepuce. The lesions over the penile shaft are tender, but the lesion over the glans penis is nontender. Serum rapid plasma reagin is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for the lesion on this patient's glans penis?
correctExplanation: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease from the spirochete Treponema pallidum that can present in multiple stages. Primary syphilis presents with a painless chancre (ulcer) of the genitalia. There are typically no systemic signs or symptoms of syphilis infection at this stage. Rapid plasma reagin can be falsely negative in the primary stage of syphilis. Dark-field microscopy of fluid from the chancre is the most sensitive test for diagnosis of primary syphilis. The treatment for primary syphilis is a single benzathine Penicillin G intramuscular injection.
incorrectExplanation: Acyclovir (Choice A) is a guanosine analog used for the treatment of herpes simplex virus or varicella zoster virus. Azithromycin (Choice B) is a macrolide antibiotic commonly used for atypical pneumonia, chlamydial sexually transmitted infections, and Bordetella pertussis infection. Ciprofloxacin (Choice C) is a fluoroquinolone used for treatment of urinary and gastrointestinal tract infections from gram-negative rods. Doxycycline (Choice D) is a tetracycline antibiotic effective against a number of gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus, Borrelia, Rickettsia, and Chlamydia.

questionStem: A 77-year-old man with alcoholism is brought to the emergency department after his landlord found him unconscious in his apartment on a hot summer day. No history is available. On arrival, he is obtunded but is responsive to painful stimuli. His temperature is 40°C (104°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Examination shows warm, dry skin and dry mucous membranes. The pupils are equally round and reactive to light; ocular movements are intact. The neck is supple. No evidence of trauma is noted. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 33%, Leukocyte count 13,500/mm³, Platelet count 75,000/mm³, Prothrombin time 13 sec, Partial thromboplastin time 50 sec, Serum Na⁺ 149 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 110 mEq/L, K⁺ 5.4 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 20 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 60 mg/dL, Glucose 50 mg/dL, Creatinine 3.5 mg/dL, Bilirubin (total) 4 mg/dL, AST 150 U/L, Creatine kinase 550 U/L, Blood alcohol 0 mg/dL, Urinalysis Blood 2+, Protein 1+, WBC 1–2/hpf, RBC 1–2/hpf, Casts few granular. An x-ray of the chest and CT scan of the head show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Heat stroke is characterized by hyperthermia, altered mental status or neurologic deficits, and variable physical signs and symptoms depending on severity. In this case, this patient was found down, in a hot apartment, presumably from the combined effects of alcohol intoxication and subsequent overheating from the environment. His exam shows tachycardia, hypotension, and warm, flushed skin. His workup reveals hypernatremia, hyperchloremia, hyperkalemia, elevated creatinine, elevated blood urea nitrogen, and elevated creatine kinase. This constellation of findings reflects hyperthermia, severe hypovolemia, rhabdomyolysis, and acute renal failure.
incorrectExplanation: Delirium tremens (Choice A) occurs 48-72 hours following cessation of alcohol use in a patient with alcoholism and is characterized by delirium, hallucinations, and autonomic instability. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (Choice C) occurs secondary to certain classes of medications, such as antipsychotics, and is characterized by hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, and autonomic instability. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Choice D) typically presents with an acute-onset, severe headache, and is shown on imaging as hyperdense material (blood) within the subarachnoid space. Thyroid storm (Choice E) presents with hyperthermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, diaphoresis, agitation, tremor, nausea, diarrhea, and weight loss, and may progress to high-output heart failure, obtundation, seizure, or coma. It typically occurs in a patient with a known diagnosis of hyperthyroidism following a secondary insult such as infection or physiologic stress from surgery or trauma. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (Choice F) occurs secondary to thiamine deficiency and is characterized by neurologic symptoms, including confusion, nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, followed by dementia and psychosis.

questionStem: A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of swelling of his left hand and redness of his left forearm, wrist, and hand after being involved in a grease fire while working at a restaurant yesterday. After emptying the fryers, a small amount of grease splattered and left small burns on his arms. He does not take any medications. He has a history of 'abnormal liver tests' and condylomata acuminata. He has had multiple sexual partners during the past 10 years and does not use condoms. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.9°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 138/68 mm Hg. A photograph of the left upper extremity is shown. There is no crepitus or fluctuance. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 18,000/mm3 with a left shift. X-rays of the left hand show diffuse soft-tissue edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: F. Lymphangitis refers to inflammation or infection of the lymphatic channels, which often occurs secondary to an infectious source at a location distal to the lymphatic channel, in this case correlating with the location of the patient’s burns. The most common cause of lymphangitis is Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A), with Sporothrix schenckii representing the most common fungal lymphangitis. Clinically, it presents with erythema in a linear, longitudinal band appearance, which correlates with the associated lymphatic drainage channel. There is also typically painful lymphadenopathy along the associated lymphatic drainage channel. This can result in pain and swelling with the possibility for high fevers.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, E, and G. Brown recluse spider bites (Choice A) are associated with dermonecrosis due to cytotoxic venom. Systemic illness is possible, more common in children, elderly, and chronically ill individuals, which can manifest with fever, rashes, and myalgias, and rarely, disseminated intravascular coagulation and end-organ damage. Disseminated gonococcal infection (Choice B) presents with pustular skin lesions, migratory polyarthralgia, and tenosynovitis. Erysipelas (Choice C) results from infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, most commonly from S. pyogenes, and on exam appears as a well-defined region of raised induration and erythema. Fasciitis (Choice D) refers to infection spreading along a deep fascial plane, most commonly from mixed flora (anaerobic and aerobic bacteria). It typically presents with acute onset of pain, which progresses to anesthesia, at a site of prior trauma or surgery. Evidence of gas production (crepitus), bullae, and severe pain out of proportion to the physical exam are indications of a necrotizing infection. Gout (Choice E) refers to monosodium urate crystals resulting in inflammatory monoarticular arthritis, classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint fluid analysis shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals, with the possibility for erosive changes of underlying cortical bone. Sporotrichosis (Choice G) results from infection by Sporothrix schenckii, a fungus, which grows within the hosties of conidia plants and is typically introduced through traumatic breakage of the skin (eg, thorn). This results in a local pustule and ulcer formation, with an ascending lymphangitis. The patient’s injury was not secondary to injury from vegetation, limiting the likelihood of sporotrichosis as the causative agent for the lymphangitis.

questionStem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She feels well. She has a 3-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Current medications include metformin and lisinopril. Her pulse is 68/min, and blood pressure is 116/74 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin A1c of 6.4%, serum creatinine concentration of 0.7 mg/dL, and serum LDL-cholesterol concentration of 112 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

choices.A: Add rosiglitazone to her current regimen
choices.B: Add simvastatin to her current regimen
choices.E: No change in therapy is indicated

correctExplanation: Simvastatin is a lipid-lowering agent that primarily reduces LDL in patients with hypercholesterolemia through the inhibition of hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA reductase. While recommendations for lipid levels vary by recommending organization, general recommendations for individuals with diabetes mellitus center around a target LDL <100 mg/dL, HDL >40 mg/dL, and triglycerides <150 mg/dL. Patients with diabetes mellitus exhibit a higher incidence of cardiovascular disease, with increased morbidity and mortality secondary to macrovascular complications such as myocardial infarction, peripheral arterial disease, and stroke. It is critical to implement lipid-lowering agents to achieve target ranges for lipoprotein levels. Treatment of LDL cholesterol levels is considered the first priority for pharmacologic therapy. Statins are the first-line treatment medication for the improvement of dyslipidemia in the setting of diabetes mellitus.
incorrectExplanation: A, C, D, and E. The goal HbA1c for a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus less than the age of 70 is 7.0%. Rosiglitazone (Choice A) is an oral hypoglycemic drug which binds to PPAR-gamma nuclear transcription factor to increase insulin sensitivity. Metformin (Choice D) is an oral biguanide hypoglycemic agent that serves as the first-line oral treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus. Neither oral hypoglycemic medication is indicated in this patient with appropriate HbA1c values. Lisinopril (Choice C) inhibits angiotensin converting enzyme, which can be utilized for hypertension management, prevention of diabetic nephropathy, and to decrease mortality in the setting of heart failure management. This patient's LDL level is currently suboptimal, requiring initiation of simvastatin (Choice E).

questionStem: A previously healthy 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of episodic memory loss, dizziness, and double vision and a 2-hour history of burning pain in his left great toe. During the past 2 months, he has had a moderate itching sensation over his legs. On arrival, he is conscious and oriented to person, place, and time. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 75/min and regular, and blood pressure is 170/80 mm Hg. Examination shows bluish-red discoloration of the left great toe. There is no pain on movement of the toe. On cardiac examination, no murmurs or gallops are heard. The spleen tip is palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 18.5 g/dL Hematocrit 62% Leukocyte count 13,000/mm³ Platelet count 420,000/mm³ Serum Urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL Ferritin 14 ng/mL Uric acid 12.9 mg/dL Which of the following interventions will most rapidly correct this patient's visual and memory disturbances?
correctExplanation: Correct Answer: E. Polycythemia vera is a chronic myeloproliferative disorder resulting in disordered, increased production of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets secondary to a JAK2 mutation. It often presents with increased pruritus, especially after hot showers secondary to increased mast cell production. Additionally, it can result in episodic severe, burning pain with red-blue discoloration secondary to blood clot formation in extremity vessels, referred to as erythromelalgia. The marked increase in red blood cell production and hematocrit can lead to the development of hyperviscosity syndrome, which presents with blurred vision and central nervous system symptoms related to vascular congestion. Therapeutic phlebotomy results in decreased red blood cell mass and blood volume, which would be the best initial treatment for reversal of the patient’s symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Aspirin (Choice A) irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes 1 and 2 resulting in decreased platelet aggregation but has no effect on red blood cell mass and blood volume. Heparin (Choice B) inhibits various clotting factors including thrombin and factor Xa after binding to antithrombin III, resulting in immediate anticoagulation, although not affecting red blood cell mass or concentration. Hydroxyurea (Choice C) inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and is used primarily for the treatment of sickle cell disease. Infusion of 0.9% saline (Choice D) would result in decreased red blood cell concentration (hematocrit), although would further increase blood volume.

questionStem: A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of low-grade fever, fatigue, and intermittent diarrhea. She has had one episode of blood in her stool and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this time. She takes no medications. Her father has hypertension, and her older sister has irritable bowel syndrome. The patient does not smoke. She drinks one to two glasses of wine monthly. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows diffuse tenderness and no rebound; bowel sounds are increased. Rectal examination shows normal sphincter tone. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Inflammatory bowel disease comprises both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation that can involve any portion of the gastrointestinal tract, manifesting with skip lesions. It particularly involves the terminal ileum and typically spares the rectum. Clinically, it can present with chronic abdominal pain, low-grade fever, weight loss, and watery or bloody diarrhea. Physical exam findings of Crohn disease include perianal fissures/fistulas, abdominal tenderness, and possible positive fecal occult blood, although bloody stools are not required for the diagnosis. Colonoscopy can demonstrate aphthous or linear ulcers with luminal strictures, inflammatory lesions, and a cobblestone mucosa. Biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis.
incorrectExplanation: A, C, D, and E. Celiac disease (Choice A) is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy resulting from autoimmune-mediated intolerance of gliadin. This results in inflammatory damage to the small bowel mucosa that primarily affects the distal duodenum and/or proximal jejunum, which leads to decreased mucosal absorption. Cytomegalovirus colitis (Choice C) occurs in patients with immunodeficiency, most commonly AIDS, and typically presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and fever, often superimposed on the patient's primary condition. Giardiasis (Choice D) presents with foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea and bloating, typically in campers who ingest cysts from standing freshwater. Irritable bowel syndrome (Choice E) presents with recurrent abdominal pain, which improves with defecation, along with a change in frequency and consistency of stool.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of a rash over her left wrist. She first noticed the rash after she started wearing a new watch, but the rash has not resolved since she stopped wearing the watch 3 days ago. She has a 2-year history of hypertension treated with atenolol. She is wearing perfume today. Examination of the left wrist shows erythematous papules. There are several new over the chest and abdomen. The skin is diffusely dry and flakes easily. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Contact dermatitis is a type IV T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction following exposure to an allergen, which results in the development of a pruritic, erythematous, and papular rash. It is characteristically distributed along the location of clothing, perfume, plant contact, or nickel jewelry contact. The rashes are often described as linear or angular in shape. In some cases, the rash can spread from the point of initial contact through transfer of the allergen by hand contact. Frequent allergens resulting in contact dermatitis are nickel, topical antibiotics, and poison ivy or oak. Diagnosis for the specific causative allergen can be made through patch testing, with first-line treatments being topical corticosteroids and avoidance of the culprit allergen.
incorrectExplanation: Atenolol (Choice A) is a beta-1 selective antagonist, used in the management of hypertension and supraventricular dysrhythmias. Side effects of atenolol include bradycardia and atrioventricular block. While perfume (Choice B) can result in a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, the patient's rash is located specifically at the site of the new watch, which likely contains a component of nickel. Her rash does not appear to demonstrate the appropriate location or timeline to be presumed secondary to the perfume. As well, given the temporal and spatial relationship to the wearing of a new watch, along with erythematous papules, this is unlikely to represent a patch of dry skin (Choice C). Contact dermatitis occurs secondary to a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which is T-cell dependent, not secondary to an impaired T-lymphocyte response (Choice E).

questionStem: Twenty-four hours after nearly drowning, a 24-year-old man in the intensive care unit has not regained consciousness. He was resuscitated at the scene and was intubated and mechanically ventilated en route to the emergency department. In the emergency department, his PO2 was 80 mm Hg on an FIO2 of 30%. An x-ray of the chest showed no abnormalities. Now, his temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 121/60 mm Hg. His respirations are 14/min on the ventilator. Examination shows no edema. Coarse airway sounds are heard on auscultation; there are no crackles. Heart sounds are distant with no gallops. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 8500/mm3, Segmented neutrophils 80%, Lymphocytes 20%, Serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis on an FIO2 of 100% and a positive end-expiratory pressure of 20 cm H2O shows: pH 7.42, PCO2 38 mm Hg, PO2 60 mm Hg. An x-ray of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current x-ray findings?
correctExplanation: Acute respiratory distress syndrome occurs in response to many etiologies, most commonly infectious, inflammatory, and traumatic. The syndrome results from the effect of cytokines on the pulmonary parenchyma from direct or indirect lung injury. This results in endothelial injury with exudative fluid extending into the alveolar space, resulting in diffuse alveolar damage and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. On chest radiographs, this is characterized by diffuse reticular and airspace opacification. In the case of drowning, aspirated fluid causes local inflammation in the lung, along with the dilution of surfactant, leading to impaired compliance and airspace infiltration. This can result in persistent hypoxia despite rising positive end-expiratory pressure and increased fraction of inspired oxygen.
incorrectExplanation: Bronchiolitis obliterans (Choice B) is characterized by chronic inflammation in the bronchioles and, in some cases, alveoli, which leads to deposition of connective tissue and can show an obstructive lung disease pattern on spirometry. Congestive heart failure (Choice C) results from increased filling pressures or impaired forward flow in the heart. This increases hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary venous circulation, resulting in transudation of fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveolar space, impairing gas exchange. It is not the most likely etiology in a previously healthy young person without cardiomegaly on chest x-ray and a more likely explanation related to recent drowning. Diffuse interstitial pneumonia (Choice D) commonly presents with infectious or inflammatory symptoms such as fever and cough productive of sputum, along with infiltrates on chest x-ray. This patient is afebrile and had a normal chest x-ray on arrival that became abnormal during the hospital course, suggesting that prior to presentation he had been healthy. Idiopathic interstitial fibrosis (Choice E), also known as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, is a restrictive lung disease that often presents in older smokers, resulting in chronic and progressive shortness of breath.

questionStem: A 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was the unrestrained driver of a car without an air bag. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 15 years. On arrival, he has severe chest pain that is most severe on inspiration. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 113 kg (250 lb); BMI is 38 kg/m2. His pulse is 130/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Examination shows an ecchymosis over the anterior chest; there is no evidence of fractures. The lungs are clear to auscultation. An x-ray of the chest shows interstitial infiltrates of the lungs bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's respiratory symptoms?
correctExplanation: Pulmonary contusions may occur after blunt or penetrating trauma to the chest. They often underlie the region of trauma to the chest wall and result from damage to capillaries with associated leakage of intravascular and extravascular fluid into the pulmonary interstitium and alveolar airspaces, respectively. This can result in hypoxia if it involves and compromises a large enough region of the lung. On chest radiographs, pulmonary contusions appear as interstitial infiltrates and/or patchy alveolar opacities. The extent and distribution depend on the mechanism, location, and force of trauma to the chest wall. Management of pulmonary contusions is supportive with control of pain, pulmonary toilet, lung expansion, and maintenance of adequate ventilation/oxygenation of the patient.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, D, and E. Fat embolism (Choice A) typically occurs following a long-bone fracture with resultant fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, petechiae, and conjunctival hemorrhage. Flail chest (Choice B) generally results when two or more adjacent ribs are fractured at two or more locations, which results in paradoxical movement of that particular segment of the chest wall. Pulmonary edema (Choice D) often occurs secondary to a hypervolemic state (eg, heart failure, renal failure, cirrhosis) or inflammatory state (eg, pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome) and can present with tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, cough, respiratory distress, and interstitial and/or alveolar opacities. Pulmonary thromboembolism (Choice E) presents with tachycardia, tachypnea, and pleuritic chest pain, and is unlikely to be related to trauma acutely, though can result from prolonged immobilization following trauma if a thrombus develops and embolizes.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of progressive shortness of breath. Examination shows decreased lung expansion, neck vein distention, and a parasternal heave; diffuse inspiratory crackles are heard on auscultation. She has 3+ pedal edema bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Cor pulmonale refers to isolated right heart failure secondary to chronic pulmonary pathology with increased pulmonary vascular resistance and right-sided heart pressures. This patient has a history of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), with decreased lung expansion and inspiratory crackles on examination, indicating the presence of underlying interstitial lung disease (ILD) and a restrictive pulmonary pathophysiology. Chronic ILD is a risk factor for the development of pulmonary hypertension. Right heart failure presents with venous congestion, seen as jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, and hepatomegaly with or without ascites. The patient exhibits all of these symptoms, making cor pulmonale secondary to ILD the most likely clinical scenario.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, D, F, G, H, and I. Angioedema (Choice A) refers to the rapid development of swelling beneath the skin or mucosa related to histamine and/or bradykinin release in the setting of an allergic exposure, use of an ACE inhibitor, or from C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency. Superior vena cava obstruction (Choice B) occurs from obstruction of venous drainage from the head and bilateral upper extremities, often related to an underlying malignancy and associated mass effect, or from thrombosis from an indwelling catheter. Biventricular heart failure (Choice C) refers to heart failure of both the left and right ventricles. Left heart failure presents with symptoms such as paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, and pulmonary edema, which are not seen in this patient. Cirrhosis of the liver (Choice D) occurs secondary to many etiologies, the most common being alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Cirrhosis presents with ascites, anasarca, jaundice, elevated transaminases, low albumin, and impaired hepatic synthetic function. Idiopathic membranous nephropathy (Choice F) is the most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome and results from many etiologies (eg, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, hepatitis viruses, systemic lupus erythematosus) and typically presents with massive proteinuria, edema, hyperlipidemia, and a hypercoagulable state. Lymphedema (Choice G) refers to swelling secondary to abnormal lymphatic drainage of a region, often secondary to surgery, radiation, or invasive parasitiasis. Myxedema (Choice H) refers to facial and periorbital swelling in the setting of hypothyroidism. Pretibial myxedema may be seen in Graves disease. Venous insufficiency (Choice I) often occurs secondary to a history of deep venous thrombosis; it can lead to stasis dermatitis and cutaneous ulcers of the affected extremity.
